Which explanation is correct?
options: Built-in functions execute in the optimized engine with no Python serialization and remain visible to the optimizer.
Python UDFs are always faster than built-in functions because they run dedicated code compiled for each transformation.
Built-in functions are exposed only in SQL; PySpark DataFrames must go through a Python UDF for equivalent logic.
Performance is identical for both approaches, so replacing the UDF is purely a matter of coding style preference.
snapshot.referenceTitle: Spark SQL built-in functions — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A PySpark job reads a Delta table into a DataFrame that currently has 200 partitions spread across the cluster. Before writing the result, the team wants to end up with 8 partitions to avoid producing hundreds of tiny output files, but without paying for a full shuffle of the data.

Which operation should they use?
options: repartition(8), the only DataFrame operation able to reduce the number of partitions
coalesce(8), which always preserves the current data distribution across the worker nodes
coalesce(8), which merges existing partitions into fewer ones without a full shuffle
either operation, because repartition and coalesce are synonyms that differ only in naming
snapshot.referenceTitle: PySpark API reference — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A junior engineer chains several DataFrame operations in a notebook: two withColumn calls, a filter on status, and a select of five columns. Each cell returns almost instantly, and she is surprised that the source table is only read minutes later, when she finally calls count(). She asks her lead what happened.

Which explanation is correct?
options: Each transformation executed immediately and stored its result; count() only aggregated the precomputed data.
Transformations are lazy and only extend the logical plan; count() is an action that triggers execution.
Actions are lazy as well; only show() forces Spark to execute the plan and read the source data.
The accumulated plan is executed automatically at cluster shutdown, when pending work is flushed to storage.
snapshot.referenceTitle: PySpark API reference — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
Two analysts on different teams must share the same SQL definition — a curated customer list built over several silver tables. The definition must live in one governed place: secured with Unity Catalog permissions, centrally versioned, and readable from any workspace attached to the metastore. The analysts use separate notebooks on separate compute.

Which object meets these requirements?
options: A temporary view (CREATE TEMP VIEW), which lives only inside the session that defines it
A global temporary view (CREATE GLOBAL TEMP VIEW), shared across sessions on the same cluster
A .sql script in a shared folder, which each analyst must open and run in her own session
A view created with CREATE VIEW in a Unity Catalog schema, stored in the metastore and governed with grants
snapshot.referenceTitle: CREATE VIEW — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
Last night, a batch job ran a faulty UPDATE on catalog.sales.orders, overwriting the status column on every row. The faulty commit landed as version 3, and the table is now at version 4. An analyst must produce a report from the table exactly as it existed before that commit, without changing the current data.

How should the analyst read the pre-UPDATE snapshot?
options: Query the historical snapshot with SELECT * FROM catalog.sales.orders VERSION AS OF 2
Run RESTORE TABLE catalog.sales.orders TO VERSION AS OF 2, then execute the report again
Run the report on the current table with a WHERE clause that filters out the overwritten rows
Read the table's underlying Parquet data files directly from the storage location with Spark
snapshot.referenceTitle: Delta Lake guide — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
An auditor must verify catalog.finance.ledger as it stood 20 days ago. The team runs the time travel query for that snapshot, but it fails with a FILE_NOT_FOUND exception pointing at a data file. The table is vacuumed weekly with the default retention settings, and OPTIMIZE also runs regularly.

What is the most likely cause of the failure?
options: Time travel preserves every version since table creation, so the failure must come from missing SELECT privileges
VACUUM only compacts small files into larger ones and never deletes any file from storage
VACUUM removed data files older than the default 7-day retention, making older snapshots unreadable
RESTORE TABLE can recover any prior version even after VACUUM has removed the underlying files
snapshot.referenceTitle: Best practices: Delta Lake — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A streaming pipeline commits new data to catalog.ops.events every 30 seconds. After a few months, the Delta table holds hundreds of thousands of small files, and dashboard queries have degraded: execution time is dominated by listing and opening files rather than scanning data.

Which maintenance action restores read performance?
options: Run VACUUM with the default retention settings, so that small files are merged into larger ones
Run OPTIMIZE, which compacts the small files into larger ones for more efficient reads
Rewrite the entire table every night with repartition(1) to produce one giant file
Scale up the compute behind the dashboards while leaving the file layout untouched
snapshot.referenceTitle: Best practices: Delta Lake — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
Every dashboard query against catalog.sales.orders derives the order date by calling to_date(order_ts) — an expression repeated across dozens of reports over billions of rows. The team wants the derived value computed once, at write time, and physically stored as a column of the table.

Which Delta Lake feature provides this?
options: A view that computes to_date(order_ts) on every read of the underlying table
A trigger that fires AFTER INSERT on the table and updates the derived column
A dashboard-level expression, so that the calculation stays out of the storage layer
A generated column: order_date DATE GENERATED ALWAYS AS (CAST(order_ts AS DATE))
snapshot.referenceTitle: Delta Lake guide — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
An operational database streams its change feed into a bronze table: each row carries the operation (insert, update, delete), a monotonically increasing sequence number, and the changed columns. In a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline, the team must keep a streaming table in sync with the current source state — deletes included — without writing manual merge logic.

Which construct should the pipeline declare?
options: A hand-written MERGE INTO statement that joins the change rows to the target on the primary key
An AUTO CDC INTO flow with KEYS and SEQUENCE BY, replacing the former APPLY CHANGES syntax
A row-level expectation that drops invalid change rows as they flow into the target table
A full refresh that recreates the streaming table from scratch whenever a new batch arrives
snapshot.referenceTitle: The AUTO CDC APIs (Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines) — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A Delta table catalog.sales.payments declares amount as DOUBLE. A new ingestion job builds a DataFrame in which amount is still STRING, with raw values like '125.50', and appends the DataFrame to the table. The job author asks what Delta Lake will do when the write is attempted.

What is the expected behavior?
options: The write fails: Delta enforces the table schema and rejects a column type that does not match
The write succeeds, storing STRING values that are converted back to DOUBLE whenever readers query
Delta automatically adds a second column, amount_string, to hold the mismatched incoming values
Delta writes only the columns whose types are compatible and silently drops the mismatched one
snapshot.referenceTitle: Delta Lake guide — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
Before promoting a new PySpark transformation into the nightly production job, an engineer wants to see what Spark intends to do with it — the planned join strategy, the filters, and the projection — without spending cluster resources actually running the query.

Which action gives her this preview?
options: Call count() after every transformation and compare the elapsed time of each stage
Nothing — lazy evaluation makes the plan unknowable until the query has fully executed
Call df.explain() to print the logical and physical plans without executing anything
Run the job in production and inspect the Spark UI, the only place where plans appear
snapshot.referenceTitle: PySpark API reference — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A reconciliation job must align catalog.sales.silver_orders with the source extract catalog.sales.latest_orders in one atomic pass: matched orders get their status refreshed, matched orders whose source status is 'CANCELLED' must be removed from the target, and unmatched source orders must be inserted.

```sql
MERGE INTO catalog.sales.silver_orders AS t
USING catalog.sales.latest_orders AS s
ON t.order_id = s.order_id
-- WHEN clauses omitted
```

Which approach meets all three requirements in this single atomic pass?
options: Run two MERGE statements in sequence: one that updates matched rows and inserts new ones, then one that deletes the cancelled orders
Use a single MERGE with WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET * and WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *, issuing a separate DELETE for the cancelled orders
Use a single MERGE with WHEN MATCHED AND s.status = 'CANCELLED' THEN DELETE, then WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *, then WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *
Replace the MERGE with an UPDATE on the matched rows followed by REPLACE WHERE, rewriting the table with the surviving and new orders
snapshot.referenceTitle: Merge data (Delta Lake upsert) — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
Over the past week, catalog.ops.shipments has behaved strangely: row counts shift overnight even though the team's own jobs were idle, and the table version keeps climbing. The engineer needs to determine exactly which operations were committed to the table, when, and by which user or service principal.

Which command gives her this commit-level audit trail?
options: SHOW TABLES with a filter on the last modified date, which lists only recent writes
A manual read of the _delta_log JSON transaction log files parsed directly from storage
The workspace audit log, which is described as the only existing record of table writes
DESCRIBE HISTORY, which lists every commit with its operation, timestamp, and user
snapshot.referenceTitle: Delta Lake guide — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
The source system exports two timestamps as STRING columns: ordered_at and shipped_at, both formatted like '2026-07-02 14:45:00'. In the silver transformation, the team must add fulfillment_days with the number of calendar days between the order date and the ship date, written in Spark SQL.

Which approach should they use?
options: Parse both columns with to_timestamp(col, 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss'), then compute datediff(shipped_at, ordered_at)
Slice fixed character positions with substring() to build year, month, and day, then subtract the dates
Convert both columns with unix_timestamp(), subtract, and divide the difference by 86400
Register a Python UDF, because date parsing requires a library that Spark SQL lacks natively
snapshot.referenceTitle: Spark SQL built-in functions — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
The table catalog.sales.order_items stores one row per line item, with columns order_id and item. An export job must return exactly one row per order, carrying all of its items in a single ARRAY<STRING> column named items — a native array, not a concatenated string.

Which query shape produces this result?
options: Explode the item column first, then concatenate the values into one delimited string
SELECT order_id, collect_list(item) AS items FROM catalog.sales.order_items GROUP BY order_id
Pivot the rows into one explicit column per item position, such as item_1 and item_2
It is impossible in pure SQL, because aggregate functions cannot return complex types like arrays
snapshot.referenceTitle: Spark SQL built-in functions — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A production Lakeflow Job that publishes Unity Catalog tables was created by a senior data engineer who left the company last month. His user account has since been removed, and the job's nightly runs now fail with permission errors when reading the source tables. The job's code and schedule are correct.

What should the team change to make the job independent of any person's account?
options: Set the job's Run as identity to a production service principal that holds the required table grants
Set Run as to the new team lead now, and to whoever leads the team after each reorganization
Leave Run as empty, since production jobs automatically run with the permissions of whoever triggered them
Grant the departed engineer's user account the workspace admin role so that its permissions are never removed again
snapshot.referenceTitle: Manage permissions on Lakeflow Jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A team maintains a shared Python module, data_prep.py, which lives in the team's Git repository and is reviewed through pull requests. Several production pipelines depend on it. They are adding a task to a Lakeflow Job that must execute this file exactly as it exists on the main branch, with no manual copies.

How should the task be configured?
options: Paste the module's current code into a notebook task and refresh that copy by hand whenever the module changes
Copy data_prep.py into the workspace first, because Lakeflow Jobs can only execute notebook tasks
Use a Python script task with the Git provider as its source, pointing to data_prep.py on the main branch
Run the script manually in a terminal on an attached cluster and load the exported CSV files afterward
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure and edit tasks in Lakeflow Jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A data engineering team must run a Lakeflow Job at 02:00 every weekday, Monday through Friday, so that reporting tables are fresh before analysts arrive. In the job's schedule settings, they open the cron expression editor to type the schedule by hand.

Which expression should they enter?
options: 0 2 * * MON-FRI
MON-FRI 02:00
0 0 2 ? * MON-FRI *
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure and edit Lakeflow Jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A task in a production Lakeflow Job got stuck in an infinite loop over the weekend. Nobody was watching, and the job stayed in the running state for three days, holding compute and blocking downstream pipelines. The team wants a stuck run like this to be stopped and marked as failed automatically.

What should they configure?
options: Nothing — Lakeflow Jobs offer no timeout setting, so a stuck run must be detected and canceled manually
The job cluster's auto-termination setting, which terminates compute that has been idle for the configured minutes
A timeout on scheduled runs only, because runs started manually with Run now are allowed to run indefinitely
A Timeout setting on the job or the task, so that exceeding the limit stops the run with a Timed Out status
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure and edit Lakeflow Jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
When a nightly Lakeflow Job fails, the team already receives an email notification. Operations, however, also needs every failure recorded in its own incident system, which exposes an HTTP endpoint, and the on-call rotation must be paged through PagerDuty. All of this should happen automatically as part of the run.

How can the team meet this requirement?
options: Keep email as the notification, since Databricks cannot target external systems, and let the incident system poll the jobs API
Add a webhook destination to the job's failure notification, so that Databricks posts a JSON payload to the endpoint
Add a final task that calls the incident system's endpoint itself at the end of every run
Switch the job to a file arrival trigger, because webhook notifications only work for event-triggered jobs
snapshot.referenceTitle: Add notifications on a job — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
The production version of an ETL notebook lives on the release branch of the team's GitHub repository. Today, a team member copies the notebook into the workspace by hand before each release, and last week's job ran a stale copy that missed two reviewed fixes. The next release must run exactly the reviewed code, with no manual steps.

How should the notebook task be configured?
options: Keep the manual copy, but add a release checklist that verifies the workspace version before each run
Leave the task pointing at the workspace, because jobs can only execute notebooks stored there
Set the task's Source to the Git provider and point it at the notebook on the release branch
Point the task at a /Repos workspace path and trust each developer to pull the release branch before the run
snapshot.referenceTitle: Notebook task for jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A Lakeflow Job runs ingest, transform, and publish as a linear chain. The team must add an alerting task that runs only when the ingest task fails — it must never run when the pipeline succeeds. The alerting code is ready; only the task's wiring is missing.

How should the alerting task be wired into the job?
options: Depends on ingest with the Run if condition All failed, so it runs only when ingest has failed
No dependencies — it runs in every run, queries the previous run's outcome through the API, and exits early on success
Depends on publish with the default Run if condition, closing the chain after every successful run
A second, identical job that contains only the alerting task and is triggered by hand when the first job fails
snapshot.referenceTitle: Control the flow of tasks within Lakeflow Jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A daily Lakeflow Job must fire at 06:00 in the company's Sao Paulo office (America/Sao_Paulo). The platform team in Paris created the schedule, so its timezone is Europe/Paris and its cron fires at 11:00 — 06:00 in Sao Paulo during the European summer. In late October, Europe ended daylight saving time, and the job began firing at 07:00 local.

How does the team make the firing time deterministic?
options: Set the schedule's timezone to America/Sao_Paulo, so the cron is always resolved in Sao Paulo time
Keep Europe/Paris and edit the cron hour by hand twice a year, when European clocks change
Set spark.sql.session.timeZone to America/Sao_Paulo in the job's tasks, so the scheduler fires in local time
Leave the timezone alone, because a job's cron automatically follows the local timezone of the engineer who created it
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure and edit Lakeflow Jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A Lakeflow Job orchestrates an end-to-end flow: a notebook task lands raw files, then a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline must process the new data, and a final task exports the curated tables. The team is now adding the middle step to the job.

How does the pipeline take part in this job?
options: As a Pipeline task, which always triggers a full refresh of the pipeline before processing
It cannot, because pipelines run only as standalone objects with their own schedules
As a notebook task that re-runs the pipeline's source notebook inside the job
As a Pipeline task that selects the pipeline and triggers a refresh — incremental by default
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure and edit tasks in Lakeflow Jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A nightly Lakeflow Job takes a processing_date parameter whose default is the current date. Late this evening, an on-call engineer must reprocess yesterday's data exactly once, and tomorrow's scheduled run must continue using the default. The job definition itself may not change.

What should the engineer do?
options: Edit the job's default parameter to yesterday's date, start the run, and revert the default before the nightly schedule fires
Clone the job into a one-off reprocess version with the new date, run it, and delete the clone afterwards
Start the run with Run now with different parameters, passing processing_date for that run only
Deploy a new bundle target that sets the parameter, since parameter values can only change through a deployment
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure and edit Lakeflow Jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A Lakeflow Job's transformations require pandas 2.x. The team has been prototyping on a shared cluster that other teams also depend on, and that cluster has pandas 1.5 pinned — upgrading it would break the other teams' workloads. The job is about to go to production.

Where should pandas 2.x be installed for this job?
options: On the shared cluster, after warning the other teams and having them retest their pipelines
With %pip install at the top of the job's notebook, which fixes the version for every job the same way
Nowhere, because pinned libraries are not supported on job clusters, so the code must avoid pandas 2.x
On the job's own job cluster, whose library list is isolated from the compute other teams share
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure clusters — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A newly hired data engineer wants to start adopting Automation Bundles for the team's Lakeflow Jobs and pipelines. They need a first bundle project on their laptop — a databricks.yml plus starter resource definitions — but have never written bundle YAML and do not want to assemble the project files by hand. Which action gets them a working scaffold the fastest?
options: Copy a full databricks.yml example out of the Databricks documentation and adapt its fields by hand each time the team starts a new project
Ask a workspace administrator to create the bundle in the workspace UI, because bundles cannot be created locally
Connect a remote Git repository to the workspace first, because databricks bundle init will not run without an existing repository
Run databricks bundle init, pick one of the Databricks-provided default templates, and answer the prompts that generate the project files
snapshot.referenceTitle: What are Databricks Automation Bundles — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A team's CI pipeline deploys every open pull request as its own Automation Bundle target — pr_142, pr_143, and so on — creating a disposable copy of the pipeline's Lakeflow Job and notebooks in a shared dev workspace. Pull request 142 has just been merged, and the pipeline must clean up that PR's deployment completely, leaving no orphaned jobs, notebooks, or artifacts, without touching other pull requests' resources. What should the merge step run?
options: Delete the shared dev workspace after every merge and let the next pull request deployment recreate everything inside it
Run nothing in the merge step — the PR deployment's job cluster auto-terminates after its runs, removing the deployed resources with it
Run databricks bundle destroy and accept its side effect of permanently deleting the bundle's source files and Git repository
Run databricks bundle destroy -t pr_142, which deletes the job, files, and artifacts that this target's deployment created
snapshot.referenceTitle: What are Databricks Automation Bundles — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A team deploys one Automation Bundle to dev and prod targets. In dev only, the group data_team must hold CAN_MANAGE_RUN on the bundle's Lakeflow Job so members can trigger and monitor runs; in prod the group must receive nothing. The team wants the grant applied automatically on every deploy and reviewed in Git like the rest of the configuration. How should this be set up?
options: Add a permissions entry granting data_team the CAN_MANAGE_RUN level on the job resource within the dev target of the bundle
Have an administrator grant CAN_MANAGE_RUN to data_team from the job's Permissions tab in the dev workspace UI after every deploy
Make data_team a workspace admin in the dev workspace so its members can run every job there without bundle changes
Skip permissions in the bundle, because bundle permissions mappings can only grant view-level access such as CAN_VIEW
snapshot.referenceTitle: What are Databricks Automation Bundles — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A team's Automation Bundle has grown into a single 600-line databricks.yml: two Lakeflow Jobs, one pipeline, and per-environment overrides for dev, test, and prod all live in one file that reviewers struggle to read. The engineers want resource definitions in their own files, with each target spelling out only what differs from the root definitions. How should the bundle be restructured?
options: Keep everything in one databricks.yml, because the bundle specification recommends keeping all resource definitions and targets together in a single configuration file
Move the job and pipeline definitions into resource files listed in the include mapping; targets inherit root definitions and override only what changes
Create a separate bundle per environment, duplicating the job and pipeline definitions in each one to keep the files short
Give up on splitting the file: a bundle cannot reference other files, so the single databricks.yml must simply be reorganized internally
snapshot.referenceTitle: What are Databricks Automation Bundles — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A nightly GitHub Actions workflow authenticates as the service principal ci-deployer and runs databricks bundle deploy -t prod, creating and updating the team's Lakeflow Jobs and pipelines in the production workspace. Security policy requires machine identities to hold the narrowest access that still lets the pipeline deploy successfully. Which privilege assignment satisfies the policy?
options: Make ci-deployer an account admin, so the nightly deploy can never fail because of a missing permission
Rely on inheritance: a service principal automatically holds the permissions of the engineer who authored the bundle
Grant ci-deployer only what the deployment needs: privileges to create and manage its jobs and pipelines, plus required catalog and schema access
Assign no privileges at all, because bundle deployments run under the workspace identity rather than the signed-in principal
snapshot.referenceTitle: What are Databricks Automation Bundles — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: An analytics team serves executive dashboards from a Medium SQL warehouse. During the morning peak, individual dashboard queries take over a minute, and the query profile shows that each query itself is resource-hungry, with high CPU and memory use per node; only a handful of queries run concurrently. The team wants each query to run faster. What should they change on the warehouse?
options: Create one dedicated warehouse per dashboard and manually route refreshes to whichever is idle
Increase the warehouse size so every query runs with more memory and CPU per node
Lengthen the auto-stop delay so the warehouse stays warm between dashboard refreshes
Recreate the warehouse from scratch, because its size is fixed at creation and cannot be edited
snapshot.referenceTitle: SQL warehouse sizing, scaling, and queuing behavior — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A scheduled notebook task fails with an uncaught Python exception. The job run page shows only the exception type and a truncated message, and the engineer needs the complete traceback together with the driver's stdout and stderr output to debug it. Where should the engineer look?
options: In the cluster's driver logs, opened from the Driver Logs tab or from delivered log storage
Only on the engineer's local machine, because driver stdout and stderr are never retained by the platform
In the Spark UI's Jobs and Stages tabs, which capture the complete Python stack trace of the failure
In the cluster metrics charts, because Ganglia-style dashboards record application-level tracebacks
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure clusters — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A Databricks SQL query that joins two gold tables and aggregates them takes minutes every night. The engineer wants a visual diagnosis: which operators dominate the elapsed time, how many rows each step produces, and whether a full table scan or an exploding join is to blame. How can the engineer get this analysis?
options: Open the Lakeflow pipeline event log, because query profiles are generated only for pipeline queries
Enable verbose mode on the warehouse first; without it the query profile never displays any operators
Open the query profile from query history: it shows the operator DAG with time, rows, and memory
Re-run the query so it is served from the query cache, then open the profile of that cached execution
snapshot.referenceTitle: Query profile — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A company's nightly Lakeflow Job cluster failed to launch: the cluster event log shows a cloud provider error stating that no instances of the requested type are available in the selected availability zone. The same instance type launched fine last week, and the job must run reliably every night. How should the team mitigate this failure?
options: Reinstall the cluster's libraries from scratch, because a corrupted dependency can block node allocation
Raise the auto-termination threshold so idle nodes remain available for the next night's launch
Audit the init script's permissions, since capacity errors are always caused by failed init scripts
Allow a mix of spot and on-demand instances, more availability zones, or alternate instance types
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure clusters — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A data engineering team runs a nightly workload of SQL queries and Spark DataFrame transformations over large Delta tables — heavy scans, joins, and aggregations. Their cluster uses a Databricks Runtime with Photon enabled, and a new engineer asks what Photon actually contributes. Which answer is correct?
options: A vectorized C++ engine that accelerates SQL and DataFrame workloads such as scans, joins, and aggregations
A compiler that vectorizes arbitrary Python UDFs so they run as fast as built-in expressions
A columnar file format that competes with Delta Lake for the on-disk layout of tables
A streaming-only accelerator that applies exclusively to Auto Loader and streaming tables
snapshot.referenceTitle: Photon — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A Lakeflow Job runs on an autoscaling job cluster configured with minimum 2 workers and maximum 8. At the start of a large backfill, thousands of tasks are queued, but the cluster runs with only 2 workers for several minutes before more nodes join. The engineer expected 8 workers immediately. What explains the behavior?
options: Autoscaling always jumps straight to the configured maximum worker count as soon as the job run starts
Autoscaling adds nodes gradually as task queues and utilization justify them; the minimum is only a guaranteed baseline
The maximum workers setting is ignored on job clusters, so this cluster can never exceed two nodes
Autoscaling does nothing by itself: an engineer must call the Clusters API and attach nodes manually as the backlog grows
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure clusters — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A data engineer must register an existing Delta dataset as an external table in Unity Catalog and runs the following statement:

```sql
CREATE TABLE main.sales.orders_ext (order_id BIGINT, amount DECIMAL(10,2))
USING DELTA
LOCATION 's3://acme-raw/orders/';
```

The statement fails with an error saying that the input path does not match any external location. What is the most likely cause?
options: The s3:// path would be accepted if the bucket were publicly readable, so the failure means the bucket policy must be opened.
The engineer's account is missing SELECT on the main catalog, and granting SELECT on a catalog is what authorizes table creation.
The path is not covered by any registered external location, an object that references a storage credential.
The statement was run on a shared cluster, and s3:// locations in CREATE TABLE only resolve on single-user clusters.
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Unity Catalog? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A data platform team plans to rename a column in main.sales.orders, one of the most widely reused tables in the lakehouse. Before making the change, the lead engineer must identify every job, query, dashboard, and downstream table that reads from it, without instrumenting any code. What does Unity Catalog provide for this need?
options: Unity Catalog captures lineage automatically, and Catalog Explorer's Lineage tab shows the table's downstream jobs and dashboards.
Lineage becomes available only after the team enables a dedicated capture job for each table that needs to be tracked.
Lineage tracks Lakeflow Jobs and pipelines but excludes queries run in Databricks SQL and the dashboards built on them.
Unity Catalog offers no lineage capability of its own, so every consuming team must maintain a manual catalog that documents its dependencies.
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Unity Catalog? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A compliance officer must produce a list of every principal that ran SELECT against the sensitive table main.hr.compensation during the last 30 days, along with timestamps. The list must come directly from a SQL query in the lakehouse: the team may not download access logs from the cloud provider or export CSV files from the query history UI. Which approach meets the requirement?
options: Ask the cloud provider for the bucket's access logs and parse the object-level entries that touch the table's files.
Query the system.access.audit system table, filtering the event date and the request parameters that name the table.
Enable query history for each user and export every user's CSV history for offline consolidation into one report.
Ask the account admin to review raw audit events manually, because audit events are visible only to admins and cannot be queried with SQL.
snapshot.referenceTitle: Audit log system table reference — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A workspace has years of legacy tables in the workspace-local Hive metastore, still referenced by old jobs using two-part names like legacy_db.orders. The company has now enabled Unity Catalog, and policy requires every production table to fall under its centralized permissions, lineage, and audit.

What must happen to legacy_db.orders to meet the policy?
options: Nothing is needed: enabling Unity Catalog automatically places existing hive_metastore tables under its governance
Run GRANT SELECT through Unity Catalog against the legacy table, which supplies the missing permissions, lineage, and audit trail
Mount the table's underlying storage with DBFS so that Unity Catalog can see and govern the data files directly
Migrate the table into Unity Catalog and update the old jobs to use its three-level name, so it becomes a UC-governed object
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Unity Catalog? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A company runs five Databricks workspaces, all in the AWS region us-east-1, and wants every workspace to see the same Unity Catalog catalogs, such as main and finance, so that grants and data stay consistent across teams. The platform lead is documenting how the Unity Catalog metastore is organized for this deployment. Which statement is correct?
options: Unity Catalog uses one metastore per account per region; all workspaces in us-east-1 attach to it and share its catalogs.
Each workspace hosts its own metastore, and administrators can optionally configure replication between the metastores.
Unity Catalog creates one metastore per catalog rather than per region, so the main and finance catalogs would each get their own metastore.
Best practice is to create several metastores in the same region and assign a dedicated one to each workspace.
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Unity Catalog? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A nightly Lakeflow Job runs under the service principal loader-sp and writes report files into the Unity Catalog volume main.ops.drop_zone. The job's identity already has USE CATALOG on main and USE SCHEMA on ops. Which grant should an administrator apply so that the pipeline can write its files into the volume?
options: GRANT SELECT ON VOLUME main.ops.drop_zone TO `loader-sp`, since SELECT is the privilege that controls reads and writes on volumes.
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON CATALOG main TO `loader-sp`, which is the least-privilege grant that still enables the file writes.
GRANT WRITE VOLUME ON VOLUME main.ops.drop_zone TO `loader-sp`, the Unity Catalog privilege that authorizes writing files in a volume.
GRANT nothing at all, because volumes automatically inherit their access rules from the storage credential backing them.
snapshot.referenceTitle: Manage privileges in Unity Catalog — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A new data engineer joins a company whose lakehouse is governed by Unity Catalog. The onboarding documentation consistently refers to tables by fully qualified names such as main.sales.orders, and the engineer asks a senior colleague what the three parts of the name mean. Which explanation is accurate?
options: main names the metastore, sales is a database, and orders is a table, following the legacy Hive database.table model with a decorative prefix.
main is the catalog, sales is a schema inside it, and orders is a table in that schema, the three-level namespace Unity Catalog enforces.
main names the workspace, sales is the database inside it, and orders is the table, matching the workspace.database.table convention.
main is the cloud region, sales is a storage bucket in that region, and orders is the table stored under that bucket.
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Unity Catalog? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A company syncs groups such as data_engineers from its identity provider to Databricks using SCIM provisioning. The governance team wants a single definition of each group, so that a grant issued in any workspace, or directly in Unity Catalog, always applies to the same members. Where should these groups be managed?
options: Recreate each group manually as a workspace-local group in every single workspace, keeping every member list synchronized by hand across the company.
Keep the groups at the account level, but accept that Unity Catalog data grants cannot reference account groups on securables.
Manage them as account groups synced from the identity provider: they can be used for grants in any workspace, unlike workspace-local groups.
Rely on the SCIM sync to create an equivalent workspace-local copy of each group automatically inside every workspace.
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Unity Catalog? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: During a quarterly access review, the governance team must list every principal that currently holds any privilege on the Unity Catalog table main.sales.orders, together with the privilege types. The reviewer wants to produce the list with one SQL statement in the query editor. How should the reviewer get the information?
options: Run SHOW GRANTS ON TABLE main.sales.orders, which lists each principal and the privilege it holds on the table.
Run DESCRIBE TABLE main.sales.orders, because its output includes the current grantees along with the table's columns.
Use the table details page in Catalog Explorer, because grants are visible there and no SQL statement returns them.
Run SELECT * FROM grants, the global view that lists every grant in the metastore without needing to name a specific object.
snapshot.referenceTitle: Manage privileges in Unity Catalog — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: During a security audit, the auditors require separation of duties across the company's Databricks deployment. They ask the platform lead to explain which administrator role manages users, groups, and workspaces at the account level, which role manages an individual workspace, and which role manages catalogs and data in the metastore. Which answer is accurate?
options: Account admin is the only built-in administrative role; workspace admin and metastore admin are just conventional names that teams use for ordinary groups.
Workspace admin automatically includes metastore admin, so a single role is enough to govern both the workspace and the catalogs in its region.
Account admins manage users, groups, workspaces, and metastores at the account level; workspace admins govern one workspace; metastore admins manage catalogs and data.
All three administrative scopes should be assigned to the same trusted person, which is what the auditors' separation-of-duties requirement expects.
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Unity Catalog? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A data engineering team's nightly Lakeflow Job runs on a classic job cluster that spends five to ten minutes launching before the first task starts. The team is evaluating moving this job to serverless compute for jobs. Which statement correctly describes what serverless compute changes for this workload?
options: Serverless compute has Databricks provision, manage, and scale the compute automatically, so jobs start quickly with no clusters to deploy or configure
Serverless compute still requires the team to create, configure, and maintain a dedicated cluster for the job before each run can start
Serverless compute can only power SQL warehouses, so it is unavailable to Lakeflow Jobs and their notebook tasks
Serverless compute removes the need for Unity Catalog to govern the tables that the job reads from and writes to
snapshot.referenceTitle: Compute — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A BI team is choosing a SQL warehouse for analysts who run ad hoc queries and dashboard refreshes with very uneven traffic: long quiet periods followed by bursts of concurrent queries. The team wants compute that starts quickly and scales responsively with that demand. Which warehouse should the team choose?
options: A classic or pro warehouse, because these provision their clusters faster than serverless warehouses and react to load spikes more quickly
Any warehouse type works, because classic, pro, and serverless warehouses behave identically in startup and scaling and differ only in price
A serverless warehouse, which starts quickly, scales dynamically, and is the type Databricks recommends for most workloads
A serverless warehouse, once the team has selected the instance types that its worker clusters will run on
snapshot.referenceTitle: SQL warehouse sizing, scaling, and queuing behavior — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A new analyst asks where each of these artifacts should live in the Databricks workspace: an iterative Python script that will be edited and run cell by cell, a SQL query that must be saved once and rerun every week, and a management-facing page of visualizations. Which guidance is correct?
options: Use notebooks for all three artifacts, since saved queries and dashboards are not workspace objects and live in separate external tools
Develop Python in notebooks, save the reusable SQL as a query in Databricks SQL, and build the management page as a dashboard
Build dashboards for all three needs, since dashboards fully replace notebooks for developing and running code
Develop Python in notebooks and build dashboards, but keep the weekly SQL in notebooks too, because saved queries cannot be shared
snapshot.referenceTitle: Introduction to the Databricks Data Intelligence Platform

snapshot.statement: Finance asks the platform team to break down monthly Databricks compute costs by team and project so that each group can be charged back. The company runs a single workspace whose many clusters and Lakeflow Jobs are shared across teams. Which approach meets this requirement?
options: Give every team its own workspace whenever possible, because compute costs can only be measured and charged back per workspace
Track costs by cluster name only, since the cluster name is the single identifying field carried into usage reports
Tag only the SQL warehouses, because custom tags are ignored on classic clusters and job clusters
Apply team and project tags to clusters and jobs, and break the tagged usage down in the billing reports
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure clusters — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A platform team must install a native operating system package on every node of every classic cluster in the workspace before notebooks or job tasks run, and manually configuring each cluster no longer scales as clusters multiply. Which mechanism should the team use to automate this installation?
options: Init scripts that run on every node at cluster startup, attached per cluster or defined globally for the whole workspace
Manual installation of the package through each cluster's library settings in the UI, repeated by hand for every new cluster
A %pip install cell in the first notebook of every job, which installs the package node-wide for all later sessions
Init scripts configured to run after each task completes, cleaning up the installed packages between runs
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure clusters — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A team's latency-sensitive Lakeflow Jobs run on classic job clusters, and every run still loses four to six minutes while cloud instances are acquired and bootstrapped. The team wants to cut that startup delay for its most time-critical nightly runs. Which approach should the team take?
options: Keep one all-purpose cluster running around the clock and point every job at it, so no job run ever waits for a cluster to start
Rely on an instance pool's pre-warmed instances, which deliver instant cluster startup with no idle-instance charges on the cloud bill
Attach the job clusters to an instance pool, which keeps idle instances ready and cuts startup time at the cost of idle billing
Move the jobs onto a pool-backed SQL warehouse, because instance pools can only accelerate SQL warehouses
snapshot.referenceTitle: Compute — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A newly hired data engineer asks how work is divided when a PySpark notebook runs on a multi-node cluster: where the notebook's code and the Spark session live, and where the actual parallel processing of data happens. Which answer is correct?
options: All of the work, including data processing, runs on the driver node; the executors are passive and only store the underlying data files
Each executor runs its own full copy of the notebook's code and independently processes its own portion of the data
Driver nodes exist only on high-concurrency shared clusters; single-user clusters and dedicated job clusters run without any driver at all
The driver node hosts the Spark session and coordinates tasks, while executors run the tasks that process data in parallel
snapshot.referenceTitle: Compute — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A finance analyst reviewing the Databricks invoice asks the platform team what a "DBU" actually is, because the bill is expressed in Databricks Units consumed per hour by each compute resource.

Which explanation is correct?
options: A fixed dollar amount that is identical across all compute types, so costs vary only with hours run
A unit of processing capability, billed per second at rates that depend on the compute type
A measure of lakehouse storage consumed, charged per gigabyte-month of data retained
A license seat billed per named user, regardless of how much compute that user runs
snapshot.referenceTitle: Compute — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A finance tool exports nightly CSV files, each starting with a header row of column names. The team loads them with the statement below, and the first run produced generic columns such as _c0 whose values are header text like transaction_id, with every data row shifted. Which change makes the load treat the first line of each file as a header?

```sql
COPY INTO main.finance.payments_raw
FROM '/Volumes/main/finance/landing/payments/'
FILEFORMAT = CSV;
```
options: Keep the statement unchanged: COPY INTO detects header rows automatically in every supported file format
Add FORMAT_OPTIONS ('header' = 'true') so the reader treats each file's first line as column names instead of data
Run a preprocessing job that removes the first line of every CSV file in the landing volume before each nightly load runs
Change FILEFORMAT to JSON, because CSV files do not accept format options such as header handling
snapshot.referenceTitle: Get started using COPY INTO — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: An insurance data source delivers one complete extract at 02:00 every night, and nothing changes during the day. Analysts refresh their dashboards once each morning, and no downstream consumer needs intraday data. A stakeholder asks why the team is not building a streaming pipeline like a competitor did. What should drive the choice between streaming and batch processing here?
options: The freshness requirement: daily refresh satisfies every consumer, so scheduled batch is simpler and cheaper; streaming pays off only when data must arrive within minutes
Industry fashion: streaming is always the recommended modern architecture for new data platforms, regardless of any actual latency requirement
Engine unification: because Databricks runs batch and streaming on one unified engine, every ingestion must now be written as a continuous streaming job
Data volume alone: the decision depends exclusively on how many bytes the source produces each night, never on how fresh consumers need the data
snapshot.referenceTitle: Batch vs. streaming data processing — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A supplier landing directory has accumulated more than 40,000 small CSV files over two years of daily deliveries. The nightly COPY INTO run keeps getting slower: most of its time now goes into discovering which files in the path are new and which were already loaded. Total daily volume is modest. What should the team conclude about this slowdown?
options: No structural limit: COPY INTO handles any file count without degradation, so the slowdown must come from warehouse sizing, not ingestion design
File size only: compacting the thousands of small files into fewer large ones solves everything, because file count never drives ingestion cost
Scale mismatch: COPY INTO suits small to medium sets of files, while Auto Loader is built for this scale, handling millions of files efficiently
Mode mismatch: Auto Loader only serves always-on, real-time streaming, so it cannot replace a nightly batch-style incremental load
snapshot.referenceTitle: Get started using COPY INTO — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: For months, a nightly COPY INTO has loaded new files from a landing volume into main.ops.bookings. During a schema dispute, an engineer drops and re-creates the table with the correct columns. The next run reloads every file still present in the landing directory, duplicating months of history. Where does COPY INTO keep its record of already-loaded files?
options: In a workspace-level ingestion service that tracks every loaded file globally, shared by all tables that read from the same cloud storage account
In the source path itself: each landing directory maintains its own tracking metadata, independent of whichever table the data lands in
In the Auto Loader checkpoint directory that backs the job, which should have been backed up before the table was re-created
In the target table's Delta transaction log: dropping and re-creating the table destroyed the loaded-file history, so everything was reloaded
snapshot.referenceTitle: Get started using COPY INTO — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A partner REST API returns orders in pages, and every response includes a next_page cursor. A nightly Lakeflow Job must fetch only orders that are new since the previous run, because reprocessing old pages wastes API quota. The job restarts on failures and its compute terminates after each run. How should the ingestion position carry over between runs?
options: Replay from the first page every night and let a MERGE against the target re-deduplicate the whole order history again on every run
Persist the newest cursor in a small Delta control table, read it at start, and pass it to the next run as a job parameter
Write the cursor to a file on the job cluster's driver disk, which survives across runs even though the cluster itself terminates
Store nothing: the partner API remembers each client's last position on the server side, so the job can simply ask for whatever orders are new
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure and edit Lakeflow Jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A nightly job pages through a partner events API that occasionally times out. The job's retry logic can re-request a page, so the same event_id sometimes arrives twice in one night; the API cannot promise exactly-once delivery. Each event must appear exactly once in the target Unity Catalog table. Which design makes this ingestion reliable?
options: Pause the pipeline until the partner can guarantee exactly-once delivery for every event_id, before writing anything into the table
Append the raw responses with plain INSERT INTO and require analysts to filter duplicate event_ids out of every downstream dashboard and report
Accept at-least-once delivery and write idempotently: MERGE INTO the target on event_id, updating matches and inserting rows that are new
Disable the job's retry logic so a timed-out call is never repeated, accepting that lost responses mean permanently missing events
snapshot.referenceTitle: Merge data (Delta Lake upsert) — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A data platform team is cataloguing the ingestion options available through Lakeflow Connect for an architecture review. One column of their catalogue must record who operates each connector: they want zero infrastructure to run themselves for standard enterprise sources, while accepting that some niche sources will run on the team's own compute.

Which classification matches how Lakeflow Connect organizes its connectors?
options: Managed connectors are Databricks-hosted and operated; community connectors are open-source packages the team runs itself
Every connector in the Lakeflow Connect catalog is hosted and operated by Databricks on serverless compute, so the team runs no infrastructure
Community connectors are operated by Databricks on the team's behalf at no additional charge
The catalog covers only databases and object storage; SaaS and streaming sources need custom code
snapshot.referenceTitle: Lakeflow Connect connector concepts — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A Structured Streaming query reads a 12-partition Kafka topic that feeds a Delta table. During traffic spikes, single micro-batches grow enormous and overwhelm the cluster. The team wants to cap how much data each micro-batch consumes and asks what controls the number of concurrent read tasks. Which configuration answers both concerns?
options: Executor count: read parallelism depends only on how many workers the cluster has, and the topic's partition layout plays no role
Topic repartitioning: changing the partition layout is the only throttling mechanism, because Spark exposes no rate-limiting option for Kafka
Manual pacing: Kafka sources cannot be rate-limited in Spark at all, so an operator must pause and resume the query during spikes
Offset cap: set kafka.maxOffsetsPerTrigger to bound each micro-batch; read tasks follow the topic's partitions, raised by minPartitions
snapshot.referenceTitle: Connect to Apache Kafka — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A bronze streaming table in a Lakeflow pipeline ingests device events. Rows with a null device_id arrive occasionally; they must never reach the table, but the team wants the failure counts visible in pipeline metrics. The current definition is:

```sql
CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE main.bronze.device_events
AS SELECT * FROM STREAM read_files('/Volumes/main/bronze/devices/');
```

How should the pipeline handle the invalid rows?
options: Add an expectation with the default warn action: invalid rows still land in the table, and only failure counts appear as metrics
Add a CONSTRAINT ... EXPECT (device_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW clause: invalid rows are dropped and their count is logged
Leave the definition as is and filter WHERE device_id IS NOT NULL in every downstream dashboard and query that reads the table
Direct all raw events into a separate quarantine table and have an on-call engineer delete the invalid rows manually after every pipeline refresh
snapshot.referenceTitle: Streaming tables (Lakeflow pipelines) — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A producer team can deliver its event feed either as Avro or as raw XML files, and it asks the ingestion team which formats can be loaded directly into Delta tables with COPY INTO or Auto Loader — without any custom parsing code — before they commit to a serialization.

Which answer is accurate for the current platform?
options: Only CSV and JSON load natively; Avro and XML must both be converted to Parquet before ingestion
Avro requires a Lakeflow Connect database connector, while XML loads directly with COPY INTO
Both load natively: formats include CSV, JSON, XML, Avro, ORC, Parquet, text, and binary files
Auto Loader reads XML, but COPY INTO is limited to CSV, JSON, and Parquet sources
snapshot.referenceTitle: Get started using COPY INTO — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: Files land in a Unity Catalog volume at unpredictable hours: some days at 08:00, some at 23:00, and some days not at all. Consumers want each delivery loaded shortly after it arrives, but the team rejects an always-on stream and refuses fixed-interval scans that mostly find nothing. Which design ingests every delivery soon after it lands?
options: A Lakeflow Job with a file arrival trigger on the volume, running Auto Loader with Trigger.AvailableNow: each run wakes on arrival, processes pending files, and stops
An always-on stream with trigger(processingTime='1 minute') on continuous compute, so a micro-batch checks for new files every minute around the clock
A cron schedule firing every five minutes that runs COPY INTO over the whole directory, accepting that most runs find nothing new
A scheduled job whose Trigger.AvailableNow step runs alongside a parallel always-on stream, because AvailableNow requires an active query to work
snapshot.referenceTitle: Trigger jobs when new files arrive — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: Two teams each start their own Auto Loader stream over the same landing directory, writing to the same Delta table, main.bronze.clicks. Each stream has its own checkpoint location and its own Lakeflow Job. Days later, the table holds exactly two copies of every ingested file. Why did the duplicates appear, and what is the correct fix?
options: Delta Lake should have detected the distinct checkpoints and deduplicated the writes; the duplicates point to a corrupted transaction log instead
Auto Loader refuses a second stream targeting the same table with a lock error, so one of the jobs must have silently skipped its files
Each stream tracks its own progress, so both discovered and ingested the same files; run a single stream per table or merge the sources
The producer uploaded every file twice into the landing directory, because separate stream writers can never create duplicates by design
snapshot.referenceTitle: Auto Loader best practices — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A landing bucket holds three years of historical files that must be loaded into a new table exactly once by a dedicated backfill run. After that run completes, ongoing arrivals must be captured incrementally by an Auto Loader stream, without reprocessing a single historical file and without backfill flags in the streaming code.

Which design meets both requirements?
options: Point the Auto Loader stream at the whole bucket with a low cloudFiles.maxFilesPerTrigger and let it chew through history first
Load history with COPY INTO and keep using COPY INTO nightly, because Auto Loader would reload everything anyway
Run one backfill batch with COPY INTO over the history, then start Auto Loader with cloudFiles.includeExistingFiles set to false
Start the stream first and run the backfill afterwards, since Auto Loader skips files loaded by other tools
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Auto Loader? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
An engineer with a background in classic Kafka consumers is setting up a Structured Streaming read from a Confluent Kafka topic and asks where the reading position — which offsets have already been consumed — is maintained for the stream, since that determines what happens after a restart.

What should the team tell them?
options: In the query's checkpoint on durable storage: offsets are committed every batch, so restarts resume from it
In the broker's consumer-group offsets topic, exactly like an application using the classic Kafka consumer
In memory on the driver, which means every restart begins from the earliest offset unless configured otherwise
In a Databricks-managed table that the team must inspect and repair manually after failures
snapshot.referenceTitle: Structured Streaming from Kafka — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
During an ingestion review, the team lists their sources: PostgreSQL, Salesforce, Confluent Kafka, Google Analytics, and a niche SaaS recruiting tool with no Databricks-provided connector. For that last source, they are evaluating vendors from the Databricks partner ecosystem rather than writing custom code.

What role do partner connectors play here?
options: Partner connectors replace Unity Catalog governance for the sources they ingest, so no grants apply to their tables
Partner connectors are required for every SaaS source, including well-covered ones like Salesforce
Partner connectors extend coverage to sources without a managed connector, through established ecosystem vendors
Partner connectors run only inside Lakeflow Jobs, executing as notebook tasks within the job graph
snapshot.referenceTitle: Lakeflow Connect connector concepts — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
Alongside the tabular feeds, a document-processing pipeline receives scanned invoices, signature images, and PDF contracts that downstream jobs will process but that will never be queried as rows and columns. The governance program still requires this data to live under Unity Catalog access control.

Where should these non-tabular files be stored?
options: As binary blobs embedded in a Delta table column, with one row created per document
In a Unity Catalog volume: /Volumes paths are governed by volume privileges
In the workspace's DBFS root, which Unity Catalog also governs by default
They cannot be governed at all, because Unity Catalog only manages tables
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Unity Catalog? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A business analyst has produced a one-off CSV extract on their laptop and needs it available to the whole team for a shared analysis. The team's storage is fully governed by Unity Catalog, the analyst has no cloud console access, and emailing the file around is against policy.

How should the file reach the team?
options: Email the CSV to the data engineering team, who each load it locally into their own sessions
Attach the file to a notebook's revision history so teammates can check it out
Push the CSV to a public cloud location and share the URL with the team
Upload it via Catalog Explorer into a Unity Catalog volume and share the governed path
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Unity Catalog? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A feed has a strict schema contract with the producing team: the ingested table must contain exactly the agreed columns, and anything the producer adds outside the contract must be captured for review rather than silently appearing in the table. The ingestion uses Auto Loader.

How should the stream be configured?
options: Supply the agreed schema explicitly with evolution off; unexpected columns then land in the rescued data column
Use schema inference with default evolution, so new columns appear immediately and visibly in the table for review
Let inference run without a schema location, which freezes the schema on the first file read
Set evolutionMode to addNewColumns and review the table's history after each run for surprises
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Auto Loader? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A managed database connector will replicate data from a production PostgreSQL instance into Unity Catalog. Of the roughly forty schemas in the instance, the team is only allowed to replicate twelve specific tables, and those tables must land in the ops schema of the main catalog — not wherever a default would put them.

What must the team configure?
options: The connector's table selection (the twelve approved tables) plus the destination catalog and schema for the replicas
Nothing beyond credentials: a managed connector replicates the full database by definition, with a fixed destination
The source table list only, because Unity Catalog always chooses destinations automatically per connector
A separate workspace per replicated table, so each lands under its own governance boundary
snapshot.referenceTitle: Lakeflow Connect connector concepts — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A nightly JDBC extraction reads a 200-million-row table from an external database and then filters it down to the last three days inside Spark. Network costs are enormous, and the external database is barely coping with the full scans.

Which change pushes the filtering work to the source database?
options: Increase numPartitions so the extraction parallelizes across more JDBC connections and the full scan finishes faster
Wrap the predicate into the dbtable subquery, so the source database applies it before returning rows
Cache the DataFrame before filtering, so the second run skips the JDBC read
Convert the read to Auto Loader and let it discover only the new rows
snapshot.referenceTitle: Query databases using JDBC — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A data provider delivers files inside a Hive-style directory layout — year=2026/month=10/day=27/part-001.json — and the ingestion team wants the year, month, and day values to become real columns of the target table without parsing file paths by hand.

Which Auto Loader capability provides this?
options: pathGlobFilter, with a glob pattern per date component applied once per ingestion
A UDF that splits the input path column on the equals sign and the year, month, and day tokens in every file
Partition inference: Auto Loader derives partition columns from the directory layout of the files
It is not possible, because directory layout information is discarded during ingestion
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Auto Loader? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A producing system can publish its events either as a continuous stream to a Kafka topic or as files dropped into cloud storage every few minutes. The consuming lakehouse team must choose one path, and both would technically work.

Which consideration should drive the choice?
options: Requirements decide: Kafka for low-latency continuous streams; file drops for simpler operation and reprocessing
Kafka should always be preferred, because it is the more modern protocol for publishing and moving event data
File-based ingestion cannot be incremental and always reloads the full history on every single run
The choice has no downstream effect, so either path is operationally equivalent
snapshot.referenceTitle: Lakeflow Connect connector concepts — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A nightly sales report joins catalog.sales.facts_sales to catalog.sales.dim_stores on store_id to append each store's region and manager. After the join, the report is missing thousands of sales: several new stores started selling before their dim_stores records were created. The business rule requires every sale to appear in the report even when store attributes are unknown.

Which join change satisfies this rule?
options: Switch to a LEFT JOIN cautiously — an outer join still discards non-matching rows before combining, so the unregistered stores would keep disappearing
Replace the INNER JOIN with a LEFT JOIN — sales whose store_id has no dimension row are kept, with NULLs filling the store attribute columns
No join change is needed — Spark inspects the table sizes and decides on its own whether INNER or LEFT semantics apply to the query
Keep the INNER JOIN and add an ORDER BY — INNER and LEFT return exactly the same rows and differ only in how the output is sorted
snapshot.referenceTitle: PySpark API reference — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A daily consolidation reads two regional extracts into DataFrames. Both extracts carry the same four columns — order_id, order_date, amount, region — but the EU file delivers them in a different column order than the US file. The combined output must pair every column with its correct data regardless of the position in which each file lists it.

How should the engineer stack the two DataFrames?
options: eu.union(us) — union() resolves columns by name automatically whenever the two schemas differ in column position
Reorder one DataFrame with an explicit select() first — manually aligning the column positions is the only safe way to combine the extracts
It cannot be done — Spark refuses to combine DataFrames whose columns are not declared in the same order
eu.unionByName(us) — it pairs columns by name between the two DataFrames, so position differences cannot mismatch the data
snapshot.referenceTitle: PySpark API reference — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
Yesterday, the query plan for the nightly reconciliation broadcast a 30 MB currency dimension next to a multi-terabyte fact table automatically — no hint appears in the query. Today the same pattern runs as a shuffle-heavy sort-merge join, because the platform team lowered the size threshold that governs automatic broadcasts of small tables in joins.

Which configuration parameter sets that threshold?
options: spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold — the size limit at or below which the planner broadcasts a join side automatically, with no hint required
No parameter is involved — automatic broadcast joins only happen when the query text includes an explicit broadcast() join hint
The broadcast threshold is a fixed engine constant — a platform team cannot raise or lower it through configuration
spark.sql.shufflePartitions — its value determines how large a table must be before the planner stops broadcasting it
snapshot.referenceTitle: Adaptive Query Execution — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
In an exploratory notebook, an engineer wants to inspect catalog.events.bronze_events, a table with roughly 200 million rows. She runs the cell below, and a few minutes later the run fails with an out-of-memory error raised on the driver process.

```python
rows = spark.read.table("catalog.events.bronze_events").collect()
```

Why did this fail, and what is the correct practice?
options: collect() fans the rows out across the executors for inspection — the driver out-of-memory error must have a different cause, such as network buffers
Prepend coalesce(1) — collapsing the DataFrame into a single partition is what allows collect() to return without exhausting driver memory
collect() ships every row into the driver's own memory — inspect with display(), take(n), or limit(), and keep full-scale processing on the cluster
The driver never holds data in Spark — only executors allocate memory, so the failure proves the executors were undersized for the table
snapshot.referenceTitle: PySpark API reference — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A gold aggregate — weekly revenue by region — is currently a plain Delta table that a nightly Lakeflow Job fully rewrites with INSERT OVERWRITE. The team is evaluating replacing it with a materialized view defined in a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline, and the lead must explain the operational difference between the two approaches.

Which comparison is correct?
options: A materialized view still requires the team to write, schedule, and maintain the refresh job that keeps its cached results up to date
A plain Delta table refreshes itself on a schedule it owns, so wrapping it in a nightly Lakeflow Job rewrites the same data twice
A materialized view is declarative — the platform refreshes it on its configured schedule, incrementally processing source changes; a table plus job keeps refresh control with the team
Materialized views and Delta tables are the same storage object — the two names only reflect whether a pipeline created them
snapshot.referenceTitle: Materialized views (Lakeflow pipelines) — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
The source system resent yesterday's events file, and the bronze table now contains rows that are exactly identical across every column — a full-row duplicate of each event. The silver table must contain exactly one row per event, and for this feed a duplicate means an exact copy of the whole row.

Which PySpark operation removes these duplicated rows?
options: dropDuplicates() — it removes rows that are identical across all columns; dropDuplicates(['event_id']) is the variant that keeps one row per key
dropDuplicates() cannot run without a column list — Spark requires the deduplication key to be specified explicitly in every invocation
distinct() — it inspects the schema and picks an arbitrary business key, such as event_id, to deduplicate the rows on its own
A row_number() window ranked over all columns — exact duplicates can only be removed by ranking the identical rows and filtering down to rank one
snapshot.referenceTitle: Spark SQL built-in functions — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A monthly revenue report reads from a table with one row per month and region: the twelve months are values in a month column. The dashboard specification now requires one row per region with a separate output column for each month — Jan, Feb, and so on — each holding that month's revenue total.

Which SQL capability produces this shape directly?
options: Hand-written conditional aggregation — twelve CASE WHEN expressions are the only way to reshape rows into columns in SQL, one per month
PIVOT — it turns each distinct value of the month column into its own output column, with the aggregation applied in the same statement
UNPIVOT — it rotates the month rows into columns and computes the aggregates while transposing the table
explode — it expands the month values across the width of the result set, giving one column per month in a single pass
snapshot.referenceTitle: Spark SQL built-in functions — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A gold orders table feeds a dashboard that averages the rating column, and stakeholders want missing ratings to count as 0 instead of NULL. The engineer preparing the aggregation must keep every order row in the output while making each NULL rating read as 0.

Which PySpark operation achieves this?
options: dropna() on rating — removing the rows where rating is NULL keeps the dashboard free of missing values entirely
fillna(0) on rating — it drops the rows whose rating is NULL, so only genuinely rated orders remain in the output
Registering a Python UDF — no built-in DataFrame operation can substitute a constant for NULL values in a column
fillna(0) on rating — it replaces each NULL rating with 0 while keeping every order row in the DataFrame
snapshot.referenceTitle: PySpark API reference — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
Phone numbers arrive in the bronze table in five different formats — '(11) 98888-7777', '5511988887777', '+55 11 98888-7777', among others. The silver contract requires every number normalized to E.164, such as +5511988887777. The transformation must run as native Spark expressions in the pipeline, with no custom code registered on the cluster.

Which function fits this requirement?
options: A Python UDF — regex-based reformatting always requires custom code registered on the cluster before the pipeline can run it
regexp_extract() — Spark's regex functions can only pull matching groups out of a string; rewriting the full value is not supported
regexp_replace() — it matches a pattern with capture groups and rebuilds the string in the normalized form in one native call
split() with a limit — cutting on every non-digit character resolves any phone format in a single pass of the expression
snapshot.referenceTitle: Spark SQL built-in functions — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A bronze table lands the amount column as STRING, with valid decimals like '125.50' and occasional junk like 'N/A'. The silver job must produce a DECIMAL(10,2) column, and every source row must survive: failed conversions should become NULL so the row can be routed to quarantine. Yesterday's run crashed with a CAST_INVALID_INPUT error on the first 'N/A' value.

Which function meets the requirement?
options: try_cast(amount AS DECIMAL(10,2)) — it returns NULL for values it cannot convert, preserving the row for quarantine routing
cast(amount AS DECIMAL(10,2)) — Spark substitutes a default 0 whenever the string is not a valid decimal number
rlike() pre-validation — a regex can confirm the format but cannot produce the typed DECIMAL column the silver contract requires
No change is needed — Spark's cast is already lenient and never raises an error when the input string is malformed
snapshot.referenceTitle: Spark SQL built-in functions — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
Compliance requires that every payment amount be non-negative. An engineer runs the statement below on a Delta table that already holds millions of historical rows, including negative refunds imported from a legacy migration:

```sql
ALTER TABLE catalog.finance.payments
  ADD CONSTRAINT chk_amount CHECK (amount >= 0);
```

What is the outcome of this statement, and why?
options: It succeeds — the CHECK applies only to rows written after it is added, and existing rows are never re-validated against it
It fails with a parse error — CHECK constraints are not supported on Delta tables, where only NOT NULL can be enforced
It succeeds — the constraint is created in a disabled, logging-only state and only starts validating once it is enabled
It fails — ADD CONSTRAINT verifies every existing row against the CHECK, and the negative rows block it until they are corrected or removed
snapshot.referenceTitle: Table constraints — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A new data architect is reviewing the team's medallion pipeline and asks the engineers to state what belongs in the silver layer and what belongs in the gold layer. The team must agree on the canonical responsibility of each layer before designing any new gold tables.

Which statement describes the two layers correctly?
options: Gold stores the raw records exactly as extracted from the source systems, preserving full source fidelity for audit and future reprocessing
Silver holds cleaned, validated, conformed data, one row per business entity; gold holds the aggregates and metrics that reports consume
Silver is the layer that serves dashboards and BI tools directly, while gold is where newly landed data first arrives for ingestion
The layers are interchangeable copies of the same data — only naming conventions distinguish one from the other
snapshot.referenceTitle: Medallion lakehouse architecture — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A silver pipeline must process only the rows that changed in a bronze Delta table since its last run — inserts, updates, and deletes alike — instead of rescanning the whole bronze table every night.
