Which mechanism provides the incremental change stream?
options: Rescan the bronze table nightly and MERGE on the primary key, accepting the full read every time
Read the bronze table as a streaming source, which surfaces updates and deletes as well as inserts
Enable change data feed and read the changes with table_changes, which returns each change with its type
Keep a hand-built control table of processed ids, refreshed by a nightly full scan
snapshot.referenceTitle: Use change data feed — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A bronze events table stores customer details in a nested column, declared as follows:

```sql
customer STRUCT<name: STRING, address: STRUCT<city: STRING, country: STRING>>
```

The silver table must expose the customer's city as a top-level column. The engineer wants the simplest native way to read that nested field, without flattening or custom code.

Which approach is correct?
options: Dot notation — select customer.address.city, which resolves nested struct fields natively in SQL and PySpark; arrays use bracket indexing like items[0]
Explode the structs first — a nested field can only be read after the entire struct has been flattened into separate rows of the DataFrame
Rewrite the transformation in SQL — PySpark DataFrames cannot traverse fields that live inside a struct column
Register a Python UDF — native functions cannot reach inside a struct, so the field must be parsed out in custom code
snapshot.referenceTitle: PySpark API reference — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A data engineer builds an intermediate DataFrame in her notebook: a read of a large Parquet dataset from cloud storage, a join with a 5 GB dimension, a filter to active regions, and a deduplication pass. Five cells later in the same notebook reuse that DataFrame, and each one currently re-runs the whole lineage, taking about six minutes per cell. She wants the reuse to be fast and the memory released when the notebook ends.

Which approach fits?
options: Call cache() before the first action runs, so that even the initial computation that materializes the DataFrame becomes faster
Call cache() in the very first cell and rely on the cached data surviving cluster termination, so that tomorrow's job run reuses it
Do nothing, because Spark automatically caches every DataFrame in memory after its first action and reuses it for free
Call cache() on the DataFrame, materialize it with an action once, and call unpersist() when the last consuming cell finishes
snapshot.referenceTitle: PySpark API reference — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
Marketing asks the data team for a very specific list: every registered customer who did not place a single order in October. The relevant tables are catalog.sales.customers, with one row per customer, and catalog.sales.orders, with many rows per order. The engineer wants a single PySpark join call that returns exactly those customers and nothing else.

Which join type should the engineer use?
options: 'left_semi', which returns the customers whose key has no match among the orders
'left_anti', which returns the customers whose key has no match among the orders
No native join type can do this; it must be emulated with a LEFT JOIN plus a filter for NULLs on the right side
'left_anti', which deletes the matching order rows from the orders table so that the customers appear unmatched
snapshot.referenceTitle: PySpark API reference — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A re-delivered bronze file duplicated customer records: the same customer_id now appears up to three times, and the copies differ in their updated_at values, so no two rows are fully identical. For the silver table, the team must end up with exactly one row per customer_id, and keeping any one of the copies is acceptable. A teammate proposes calling distinct() on the bronze DataFrame.

What is the difference between the two candidate calls?
options: distinct() compares every column, so rows that differ in updated_at all survive; dropDuplicates(['customer_id']) keeps a single row per key
distinct() and dropDuplicates() are interchangeable, so the teammate's call would already deduplicate on the customer_id key
distinct() accepts a column list, as in distinct('customer_id'), and deduplicates on just the columns passed to it
dropDuplicates(['customer_id']) cannot work by itself; it must be combined with a row_number() window to pick the surviving row
snapshot.referenceTitle: Spark SQL built-in functions — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
An analyst joins customers to loyalty_accounts on customer_id and is surprised to see that customers whose customer_id is NULL disappear from the output. The join call passes no join type:

```python
customers.join(loyalty_accounts, "customer_id")
```

A teammate argues that switching to a left join will not help, because a NULL key never matches anything anyway. Which statement is correct?
options: NULL is treated as equal to NULL in the join, so those customers did match loyalty rows that also carry a NULL key
A join whose key column contains NULL fails outright with an error, and those rows were rejected while all the other rows joined normally
NULL never satisfies an equality comparison, so the default inner join drops those rows — a left join would keep them, padded with NULLs
Spark converts NULL keys to empty strings before joining, so the customers survive in the output under a different value
snapshot.referenceTitle: PySpark API reference — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A monthly revenue report must show one row per month with two separate columns, web_revenue and store_revenue. The source is a large orders table with the columns event_month, channel, and amount, and the report must compute both totals in a single pass over the table.

Which construct computes the two metrics in one aggregation?
options: One query per channel, each filtering WHERE channel = 'web' or WHERE channel = 'store', whose result sets are combined into the report afterwards
GROUP BY channel with SUM(amount), which yields one row per channel carrying that channel's revenue total
PIVOT on channel, which is limited to count aggregations and therefore cannot produce revenue sums per channel
SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE channel = 'web') and SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE channel = 'store') within one GROUP BY event_month
snapshot.referenceTitle: Spark SQL built-in functions — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
The bronze orders table stores an ARRAY<STRING> column named coupon_codes. The attribution notebook needs one row per order_id and coupon pair, but many orders carry no coupons at all — their array is empty or NULL — and those orders must still appear in the output, with NULL in the coupon position, so that order totals reconcile.

Which expression should the notebook use?
options: explode(coupon_codes) — rows whose array is empty or NULL are preserved, with NULL in the generated column
explode_outer(coupon_codes) — rows whose array is empty or NULL are preserved, with NULL in the generated column
posexplode(coupon_codes) — as the positional variant of explode, it is the one that preserves rows with empty or NULL arrays
No generator is safe here — an empty array aborts the query, so orders without coupons must be filtered out before exploding
snapshot.referenceTitle: Spark SQL built-in functions — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A reporting query must return every order, joined to its payment when one exists, while showing only approved payment details:

```sql
SELECT o.order_id, p.status
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN payments p ON o.order_id = p.order_id
WHERE p.status = 'APPROVED';
```

After running it, the analyst notices that orders without any payment are missing from the results. Why did they disappear, and what is the fix?
options: The WHERE clause runs after the join: NULL-padded orders fail p.status = 'APPROVED', turning the LEFT JOIN into an inner join — move the predicate to ON
ON and WHERE are interchangeable in outer joins, so the missing orders must have been lost by a different filter somewhere upstream
Spark automatically rewrites WHERE predicates on the right table into the ON clause, so rewriting the query manually is pointless
A LEFT JOIN by definition never returns orders that lack a matching payment; preserving them requires a FULL OUTER JOIN instead
snapshot.referenceTitle: PySpark API reference — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
The weekly engagement report counts reviews with the expression SELECT count(comment_text) FROM catalog.reviews. The reported number comes out lower than the table's actual row count, and QA confirms that many customers submit a star rating only, leaving comment_text NULL. The report must count every review.

Which expression and explanation are correct?
options: count(comment_text) counts every row, NULLs included, so the missing reviews must be dropped somewhere else in the pipeline
count(*) skips any row that contains a NULL in one of its columns, so both expressions under-report on nullable tables
count(expr) counts only rows where expr is not NULL; count(*) counts every row, so the report needs count(*) to total all reviews
count(*) and count(col) are equivalent and always return the same number, so the shortfall must come from a stale result cache
snapshot.referenceTitle: Spark SQL built-in functions — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A nightly reprocessing job was accidentally deployed with this write and, on its first run, replaced an entire silver table with only a partial re-run's worth of data:

```python
df.write.mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("catalog.sales.silver_payments")
```

The team now wants every reprocessing job to fail loudly instead of touching a table that already exists. Which save mode gives that behavior?
options: append, which replaces the table's previous contents with each new batch that gets written
overwrite, which refuses to write whenever the target table already contains any data at all
No save mode is needed, because Delta treats the modes as advisory hints and always appends the incoming data atomically
errorIfExists, the default save mode, which makes the write fail if the target table already exists
snapshot.referenceTitle: Best practices: Delta Lake — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A late-arrival job rebuilds only yesterday's slice of the events table, which is partitioned by event_date. In a single write, it must atomically replace only the rows whose event_date equals '2026-07-02' and leave every other day of the table untouched; the job's output DataFrame contains just the rebuilt day.

Which write approach meets both requirements?
options: Run DELETE on the day's rows and then INSERT the corrected batch afterwards — each statement is atomic on its own, and together they cover the day
Write with mode('overwrite') and no further options — the whole table is replaced atomically, which also refreshes yesterday's rows
Write with mode('overwrite') and option('replaceWhere', "event_date = '2026-07-02'") — only the matching rows are replaced, in one atomic commit
Convert the table to external storage first, because replaceWhere cannot operate on Unity Catalog managed tables
snapshot.referenceTitle: Best practices: Delta Lake — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
Every night, a MERGE synchronizes catalog.sales.silver_orders with the source extract, updating matched orders and inserting new ones:

```sql
MERGE INTO catalog.sales.silver_orders AS t
USING catalog.sales.source_orders AS s
ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *
```

Orders are sometimes deleted in the source, and those deletions must also disappear from silver_orders, in the same atomic statement. Which clause adds this behavior?
options: WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE — it applies to the target rows whose keys have no counterpart in the source table
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN DELETE — that clause already covers the target rows that are absent from the source
None: every MERGE clause can only act on rows of the source, so unmatched target rows are out of the statement's reach
Deletion is outside MERGE's scope, so schedule a separate DELETE ... WHERE order_id NOT IN (SELECT ...) after every merge runs
snapshot.referenceTitle: Merge data (Delta Lake upsert) — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
An ingestion job appends a DataFrame to catalog.sales.customers, an existing Delta table. This week the source schema added a new column, loyalty_tier, and the append now fails Delta's schema enforcement. The team wants the write to succeed by adding the new column to the table, and no existing rows should be rewritten.

Which write option achieves this?
options: Use .option('overwriteSchema', 'true'), which adds the new column to the table while leaving every previously written row untouched
Use .option('mergeSchema', 'true'), which evolves the table schema additively — the new column is added with no rewrite
Use a TBLPROPERTIES change that turns schema enforcement off permanently, so that no write option is ever needed again
Use mergeSchema, keeping in mind that it also drops table columns that the incoming DataFrame no longer carries
snapshot.referenceTitle: Best practices: Delta Lake — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
Years of analytics history live as Parquet datasets in the company's cloud storage lake. Governance now requires these datasets to become Delta tables, so that the lakehouse gains ACID transactions and time travel on top of them, but the data files must stay exactly where they are — no copies, no rewrites, no new storage locations.

Which approach meets the requirement?
options: Run CREATE TABLE AS SELECT over each dataset, copying the rows into newly written Delta files under a managed location
Run CONVERT TO DELTA, which copies the existing Parquet files into the table's managed storage location first
Register the datasets as plain external Parquet tables instead — Parquet already guarantees ACID transactions, so converting them adds nothing
Run CONVERT TO DELTA on each dataset — Delta builds its transaction log over the existing files in place, without copying them
snapshot.referenceTitle: Delta Lake guide — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
The development team wants a safe sandbox for risky experiments: a copy of the 100 TB production table catalog.sales.orders that they can transform, rewrite, and even corrupt without consequences. Storage costs must not double, and any commits made on the copy must never affect the production table.

Which approach fits?
options: CREATE TABLE dev.orders AS SHALLOW CLONE catalog.sales.orders — the clone reuses the existing data files while keeping independent metadata and history
CREATE TABLE dev.orders AS DEEP CLONE catalog.sales.orders — a deep clone shares the underlying data files with the source table
CREATE TABLE dev.orders AS SELECT * FROM catalog.sales.orders — a full physical copy is unavoidable whenever dev writes must remain isolated from production
A shallow clone works only for read-only experiments: it keeps inheriting every later commit made on the source, so dev writes would flow back
snapshot.referenceTitle: Delta Lake guide — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A monthly reconciliation must compare the bank statement feed with the ledger: every row from either side must appear in the output, matched rows side by side, and rows present on only one side kept with NULLs on the other.

Which join produces this result?
options: A FULL OUTER JOIN keeps rows from both sides, matching on keys and filling NULLs otherwise
An INNER JOIN on transaction_id, which guarantees that every row of both sides appears in the result
A LEFT JOIN of bank against ledger, which keeps unmatched ledger rows as NULLs
A UNION of both feeds, which places corresponding rows side by side for comparison
snapshot.referenceTitle: PySpark API reference — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A Lakeflow Job starts with a notebook task, `pick_tables`, which scans operational metadata and computes the exact list of bronze tables that need a rebuild — a different list every night:

```python
dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set(key = "tables", value = tables)
```

The next step must run the rebuild notebook once for every table in that list. How should the For each task that follows `pick_tables` be configured?
options: Point its Inputs field at the task value reference {{tasks.pick_tables.values.tables}}, so the loop follows the list pick_tables produced
Copy the table names from last night's run into the Inputs field as a static JSON array, and edit the job whenever the list changes
Hardcode a master table list in the job definition, because For each inputs cannot reference values from other tasks
Drop the For each task and use a single notebook task that reads the array from pick_tables and loops over the tables with a Python while loop
snapshot.referenceTitle: Use a For each task to run another task in a loop — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
An operations dashboard is published in the workspace, and the first analyst to open it each morning waits while all of its queries run from scratch. The team already runs a scheduled Lakeflow Job that finishes refreshing the underlying tables by 07:00, and they want the dashboard's results ready before analysts arrive at 08:00.

What should the team add to this job?
options: Nothing, because a published dashboard refreshes its results only when a user opens it, and no job task can change that
A Dashboard task after the table refresh, which refreshes the published dashboard's results as a step of the job
A notebook task that exports the dashboard to a PDF every morning, because only an export forces the dashboard's queries to run
A Dashboard task that publishes a new copy of the dashboard on every run, so analysts always open a freshly published version
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure and edit tasks in Lakeflow Jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A Lakeflow Job runs two slow loads in parallel after the same extract task: load_customers and load_orders have no dependency on each other, and both must stay concurrent to fit the nightly window. A final task, run_quality_checks, must execute exactly once, only after both loads have completed successfully.

How should run_quality_checks be wired?
options: Chain extract, load_customers, load_orders, and run_quality_checks in a strict line, because only linear chains can make a task wait for two others
Attach run_quality_checks to whichever load finishes first, and let it start as soon as that single branch completes
Split the checks into two tasks, one per branch, because a single task cannot depend on more than one upstream task
Make run_quality_checks depend on both load_customers and load_orders, keeping the default All succeeded run-if condition
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure and edit tasks in Lakeflow Jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A Lakeflow Job has six tasks — notebooks, one Python script, and one SQL file — that all live in the same GitHub repository on the release branch. Setting the repository and branch on every task is repetitive, and last month two tasks were accidentally pointed at different branches.

How should the job's source be configured?
options: Configure the repository and branch once as the job's Git source, and have tasks reference only paths relative to the repository root
Repeat the full repository URL and branch on every task, since each task must carry its own complete source settings
Skip Git for this job, because remote Git sources can only be configured on individual tasks, never at the job level
Rewrite the SQL file task as a notebook task, because jobs that use a Git source cannot include SQL tasks
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure and edit Lakeflow Jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A data engineer is editing a production Lakeflow Job in which the notebook task B already depends on the notebook task D. To make the two steps verify each other's output, the engineer adds a dependency in the opposite direction, configuring task D to depend on task B as well, and clicks Save.

What is the result?
options: The cycle is accepted, and the two tasks re-run in a loop until both finally succeed
The cycle is accepted, but the loop executes only once per run, after which the job continues with the downstream tasks
The dependency is accepted because both tasks are notebooks, and notebook tasks are allowed to close dependency cycles
The configuration is rejected: task dependencies must form a directed acyclic graph, and a cycle cannot be saved
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure and edit tasks in Lakeflow Jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A data engineering team runs the same preparation pipeline for a morning report. Business users need it at 06:00 from Monday through Friday, while the Saturday data cut happens later, so the pipeline must run at 08:00 on Saturdays. The team wants one job definition, one run history, and one place to change the code.

How should the job be configured to fire on both schedules?
options: Add two scheduled triggers to the job: a weekday 06:00 cron and a Saturday 08:00 cron
Clone the job into two identical jobs, each with its own schedule, and maintain both in parallel
Keep a single trigger, because one Quartz cron expression can fire at different times on different days
Leave the weekly schedule as-is and rely on its automatic retries to produce the Saturday 08:00 run
snapshot.referenceTitle: Automate jobs with schedules and triggers — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A platform team's master Lakeflow Job coordinates the company's onboarding flow. One step must launch the partner team's onboarding job, wait for its outcome, and let downstream tasks in the master job run only if that job succeeded. The partner's job stays owned and scheduled by the partner team.

How should the master job trigger the partner's job?
options: Use a notebook task that calls the Jobs REST API to start the partner's job and poll for its result
Use a pipeline task pointing at the partner's job, since pipeline tasks can execute any existing job
Use a Run Job task that starts the partner's job, so its outcome becomes a step in the master DAG
Use a manual handoff, because Lakeflow Jobs cannot launch other jobs in a managed way
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure and edit tasks in Lakeflow Jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A Lakeflow Job declares a job-level parameter target_date, and one of its notebook tasks declares a task parameter with the same key target_date but a different default. An on-call engineer then triggers the job with Run now, passing their own value for target_date.

Which value does that task receive?
options: The task parameter's default, because task-level settings are always the most specific
The job parameter's default, because job-level settings override everything including Run now
An error at run time: declaring the same parameter key at two levels is rejected by the platform
The Run now value wins; below that, the job-level parameter beats the task parameter on a shared key
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure and edit Lakeflow Jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
Governance rules at a company state that compute used by Lakeflow Jobs must follow approved shapes: permitted node types and a maximum worker count. The platform team wants these rules enforced automatically whenever engineers configure compute for their jobs, not reviewed case by case.

What should the platform team do?
options: Apply a compute policy to the job compute, so permitted node types and size limits are enforced
Document the approved shapes in the team wiki, because compute policies apply only to interactive all-purpose compute
Rely on automatic inheritance, because every job takes the compute policy of the engineer who created it
Cap the number of clusters per workspace, because compute policies control only how many clusters can exist
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure clusters — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A team is migrating an old ETL process to Lakeflow Jobs. Today one long notebook chains five processing stages with %run: each stage calls the next notebook, everything shares a single execution, and a failure in stage three means rerunning the whole chain the next morning.

What is the main benefit of rebuilding this chain as separate notebook tasks in one job?
options: The ability to keep a single shared execution, since chained %run notebooks are the recommended pattern for production
The ability to keep the %run chain, because jobs cannot run notebooks as separate tasks
The ability to retry, monitor, and branch each stage independently, and rerun only the failed stage
The ability to preserve %run behavior exactly, with less configuration to maintain than separate tasks
snapshot.referenceTitle: Notebook task for jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A source system that feeds a nightly Lakeflow Job will undergo maintenance tomorrow, and the team decides the job should not fire while the data is unstable. Today's run has already started and is still in progress. The job definition, its run history, and next week's schedule must all be preserved.

What should the team do?
options: Cancel the in-progress run immediately, because pausing a job also kills every run that is still active
Pause the job's scheduled trigger: it stops starting new runs, and the active run still finishes
Remove the schedule from the job definition and re-enter it by hand after the maintenance window
Delete the job and rebuild it after maintenance, because stopping firings requires deleting the job
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure and edit Lakeflow Jobs — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
The first task in a Lakeflow Job runs a SQL task that computes yesterday's totals; a downstream notebook task needs that number as a parameter, but the SQL task does not use dbutils, so it cannot set a task value itself.

How can the SQL task's output reach the notebook task?
options: Have the SQL task write the value with dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set in a trailing statement
Pull it with a dynamic value reference like {{tasks.totals.output.first_row.yesterday_total}}
Recompute the total in the notebook with an identical SQL query against the same tables
Declare the number as a job parameter and edit the job definition manually every single night
snapshot.referenceTitle: Use dynamic value references — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A downstream Lakeflow Job must refresh whenever two specific upstream tables change — sales.orders and sales.returns — but a third table in the same schema, sales.staging, changes constantly and must never trigger the job.

How should the table update trigger be configured?
options: Monitor the whole sales schema, and cancel any run that was triggered by sales.staging
Select sales.orders and sales.returns as the trigger's monitored tables, so only they fire the job
Add a filter in the job's first task that checks which table changed before continuing
Rely on the default behavior, because table update triggers always watch every table in the source schema
snapshot.referenceTitle: Trigger a job when a table updates — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A team configures a file arrival trigger by pasting the raw cloud URL of an S3 bucket where a vendor drops CSV files: s3://vendor-drops/incoming/. The trigger setup fails, and the team asks what location it can actually monitor.

What is the requirement?
options: Any s3:// path works as long as the bucket is in the same region as the workspace
Triggers can only watch workspace DBFS paths, so the vendor must upload everything to /FileStore instead
The raw bucket URL works if the team also pastes AWS access keys into the job definition
File arrival triggers monitor a Unity Catalog volume or registered external location path, not arbitrary URLs
snapshot.referenceTitle: Trigger a job when a file arrives — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A data engineer fixes a null-handling bug in the silver_orders notebook inside the team's Git folder, which is cloned from the team's remote repository and has the feature/null-fix branch checked out. They finish the edit and must send the change to the remote repository so a teammate can review it, without leaving the Databricks workspace. What should the engineer do?
options: Open the Git dialog, review the highlighted changes, add a commit message, and click Commit & Push to send the branch to the remote
Push the change with Git on a local machine, because the workspace UI can edit notebooks but cannot push commits
Save the notebook and wait: the Git folder commits every change automatically and pushes it to the checked-out branch
Use the Git dialog only to browse the branch history, because it shows past commits but cannot create new ones
snapshot.referenceTitle: Git operations with Git folders — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A data engineer uses the Databricks CLI on a laptop that runs commands against both the team's development workspace and the production workspace. They are tired of re-typing credentials and want a fast, explicit way to choose which workspace a command targets. How should the engineer configure the CLI?
options: Rely on the browser session signed in to the workspace, since the CLI can only reach that one workspace
Add a named configuration profile per workspace to ~/.databrickscfg and select it with --profile or -p
Accept a single host per machine, because the CLI supports only one workspace URL in its configuration
Avoid environment variables entirely, because DATABRICKS_HOST and DATABRICKS_TOKEN are not recognized by the CLI
snapshot.referenceTitle: Databricks CLI — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A team's CI log shows this command completing successfully, with no target specified:

```bash
databricks bundle validate
```

A junior engineer expected the command to fail without -t and is surprised that the output mentions target dev. Why did the command validate the dev target?
options: It validates all targets declared in the bundle configuration one after another in a single pass
It errors out, because every bundle command requires an explicit --target option
It uses the target marked default: true in the bundle configuration, which is dev here
It always validates the production target first, because that is the safest default
snapshot.referenceTitle: What are Databricks Automation Bundles — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A team's Automation Bundle defines one Lakeflow Job and its notebooks. The team promotes releases through development, staging, and production workspaces and must guarantee that the exact code revision that passed staging tests is what runs in production. Which promotion approach provides that guarantee?
options: Keep a separate branch per environment, so each workspace always deploys its own copy of the code
Merge the development branch straight into the production branch whenever a release is due
Deploy staging's workspace files to production by copying the tested folders in the workspace UI
Deploy the same bundle commit to each target in turn; only target-level variables and overrides differ between environments
snapshot.referenceTitle: What are Databricks Automation Bundles — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A company's data platform runs on Bitbucket, and the platform lead wants to manage pipeline notebooks in Databricks Git folders connected to the company's Bitbucket repositories. Before planning the rollout, the lead asks which Git providers Git folders support. What is the correct answer?
options: GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps (Azure Repos), Bitbucket Cloud, and Bitbucket Server and Data Center are all supported
Only GitHub repositories can be connected, so the team must mirror its Bitbucket repositories to GitHub
GitLab and Bitbucket require a third-party connector purchased from a Databricks partner
Any Git hosting service works with no restrictions, including self-hosted servers on any network
snapshot.referenceTitle: Git folders concepts — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A team deploys one Automation Bundle to three targets: dev, test, and prod. Each target is a different Databricks workspace, and the team must keep each environment's deployed files and state separate so deployments never collide. Where should the per-environment workspace host and paths be defined?
options: In fixed global paths that every target shares, because one bundle uses one workspace location
In three separate bundles, one per environment, each shipping its own folder layout
In each target's workspace mapping, declaring that environment's host together with root_path and artifact_path
Nowhere: the workspace is chosen by whichever configuration profile happens to be active in the deployer's terminal
snapshot.referenceTitle: What are Databricks Automation Bundles — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: An Automation Bundle deploys a Lakeflow Job whose Python task must call an external API with a bearer token. Security policy forbids the token from appearing in any versioned file or in the deployed job's visible configuration. The bundle files live in Git. How should the task get the token?
options: Declare a bundle variable for the token and pass its value with --var each time the pipeline deploys
Point a task environment variable at a secret scope with a reference like {{secrets/scope/key}}, resolved at run time
Commit a placeholder string in the YAML and have the CI pipeline rewrite the file with sed right before the deploy step runs
Keep the token directly in the YAML, since the team's Git repository is private to the platform group
snapshot.referenceTitle: What are Databricks Automation Bundles — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A company keeps all of its data products in one large monorepo. The orders team only needs the /products/orders directory — its notebooks and job definitions — available in a Databricks Git folder, not the entire repository. How should the team create the Git folder?
options: Create it normally: a Git folder always clones the full repository, and unused directories must simply be ignored
Tell the team that monorepos are not supported and the product must move to its own repository
Maintain a mirror repository that contains only the orders product, and connect the Git folder to the mirror
Enable sparse checkout when creating it and set the cone pattern to /products/orders, cloning only that subset
snapshot.referenceTitle: Git folders concepts — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: While developing ingestion notebooks locally in an IDE, a data engineer wants their local project folder and a folder in the Databricks workspace to stay in step as files change, and asks whether the CLI's sync command keeps both sides identical. What does databricks sync actually do?
options: It synchronizes one way, local directory to workspace folder; edits made in the workspace never flow back
It synchronizes in both directions, keeping the local project folder and the workspace folder identical at all times
It replaces Automation Bundle deployments, pushing project files straight into production workspaces
It copies local files into DBFS paths such as dbfs:/tmp, since it cannot write to workspace folders
snapshot.referenceTitle: Databricks CLI — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A new data engineer has only seen the Databricks CLI used to deploy Automation Bundles and assumes that bundles are all it is for. The team lead wants to correct this with an accurate description of what the CLI covers. Which description is accurate?
options: The CLI is a bundle-only tool: it validates, deploys, and runs Automation Bundles and nothing else
The CLI runs exclusively inside the Databricks workspace and cannot be installed on a laptop
The CLI wraps the platform's REST APIs, managing clusters, jobs, pipelines, files, permissions, and more
The workspace UI can do everything the CLI does just as conveniently, so the CLI adds no real capability for teams
snapshot.referenceTitle: Databricks CLI — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A team's Automation Bundle defines a Lakeflow Job whose notebook task references a project file, notebook_path: ../src/ingest.py. The bundle deploys to the dev target for the first time, and an engineer asks where ingest.py ends up so they can trace what the job actually runs. Where do the bundle's files go at deploy time?
options: The job reads the file straight from the Git provider at run time, so no copy ever lands in the workspace
The deploy uploads the files into the target workspace's bundle paths, and the deployed job points at those copies
The files stay on the engineer's machine, and the job fetches them from there whenever it runs
The deploy creates a Git folder in the target workspace that holds the project's files for the deployed job to pull from
snapshot.referenceTitle: What are Databricks Automation Bundles — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: Minutes after a routine deploy of the prod target, dashboards show that a change in the release broke a downstream metric. The team must restore production to the last-known-good version of the bundle quickly and cleanly. What should they do?
options: Run databricks bundle rollback -t prod to restore the previous deployment automatically
Delete the affected jobs and pipelines in the production workspace and let the owning teams rebuild them by hand
Select the last-known-good deployment from the versions the bundle keeps in the workspace and re-apply it
Revert the bad commit in Git and redeploy prod; the bundle then overwrites the resources with the restored code
snapshot.referenceTitle: What are Databricks Automation Bundles — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: One bundle serves several CI pipelines, and each runner needs a slightly different value for the same setting — for example, the catalog prefix the deployed pipeline writes to. The team wants to keep a single databricks.yml and avoid per-pipeline copies of the configuration. How can the differing values be supplied?
options: Declare the differing values as bundle variables and supply each runner's values through BUNDLE_VAR_-prefixed environment variables
Hardcode every value, because bundle configuration files cannot read anything from the environment
Generate a different databricks.yml for each pipeline, with each runner's value written into its own file
Use environment variables only to choose the workspace host, because that is the only setting they can affect
snapshot.referenceTitle: What are Databricks Automation Bundles — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A GitHub Actions runner runs Databricks CLI commands on every merge to main. DATABRICKS_HOST is already set to the workspace URL, the team has created the service principal ci-release with an OAuth secret, and the workflow must act as that service principal with no interactive sign-in. What must still be configured on the runner?
options: A weekly calendar reminder for an engineer to run databricks auth login interactively on the runner
The username and password of a platform engineer as workflow variables for the CLI to authenticate with
The service principal's client ID and secret as DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID and DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET, so the CLI runs OAuth M2M
A personal access token that belongs to a human administrator, because service principals cannot authenticate the Databricks CLI
snapshot.referenceTitle: Databricks CLI — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A data engineer is new to the Databricks platform and wants to study a slow PySpark notebook run in the Spark UI. The engineer wants to start from the actions the notebook triggered, open the slowest one, and then see how many tasks each of its stages ran and how long every task took. Which navigation matches how the Spark UI organizes this information?
options: The Jobs tab lists the triggered actions; a job page shows its stages; the Stages view lists each stage's tasks with durations and I/O metrics
The Storage tab reports how long every task ran inside each stage, next to the cached tables that those tasks read
The Executors tab displays the execution plan of each action, including stage boundaries and per-task assignments
The Jobs and Stages tabs are the same view, with Stages only adding extra filters by duration and status
snapshot.referenceTitle: Spark UI guide — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: An all-purpose cluster that hosts the team's interactive notebooks was restarted overnight: sessions died, and the uptime counter had reset by morning. The engineer did not schedule any restart and wants to reconstruct exactly what happened to the compute while nobody was watching — whether it was resized, terminated, or failed, and at what time. Where is that record kept?
options: In the job run history, which records every cluster lifecycle event — creations, resizes, terminations — of the compute that jobs used
In the cluster event log, which is written only for job clusters and never for all-purpose compute
In the cluster event log, which records timestamped events such as creation, resizes, terminations, and failures
In no view at all, because the platform does not persist cluster-level events like restarts or resizes
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure clusters — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: Databricks SQL dashboards have been intermittently slow for a week. The team lead wants to review the slowest queries that one specific analyst ran on the shared warehouse last Tuesday, see how long each took, and check whether they were queued or spilling. How can the lead find them without leaving the workspace UI?
options: Ask the analyst to export her own list manually, since each user's history is private and no consolidated view exists for the team
Open Query History, filter by user, warehouse, and date range, then sort the runs by duration to surface the slowest
Open a query profile, which lists every query in the workspace ranked by elapsed time and spill
Rerun each dashboard query by hand, because query history is discarded as soon as execution finishes
snapshot.referenceTitle: Query history — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A dashboard query against two gold Delta tables finished in about 40 seconds when the warehouse was cold. Minutes later, the exact same query returned in two seconds, although no files had changed. The team concluded that the warehouse 'warmed up' and now expects every rerun to be fast. What actually explains the second run?
options: The result cache is global to the account and never expires, so any user running any similar query gets the two-second answer
The cached result also covers queries with different filters over the same tables, which are answered without re-execution
The query was re-executed in the background at higher priority, and the cache only duplicates its profile in query history
The result cache served the identical query without re-execution, since the underlying tables had not changed
snapshot.referenceTitle: Query profile — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A streaming workload ingests Kafka events into a streaming table through a continuously running query. Throughput seemed to drop after a configuration change, and the engineer wants to confirm, on the live query, how many input rows per second the source is delivering and how long each micro-batch takes to process. Where should the engineer look?
options: The Structured Streaming tab of the Spark UI, which shows active queries with input rate and batch duration statistics
No Spark UI tab, because streaming queries are deliberately excluded from every view of that interface
A StreamingQueryListener registered in the query's code, which is the only way to observe input rates and batch durations
The Lakeflow job run history page, the sole view that reports per-query stream metrics like rows per second
snapshot.referenceTitle: Spark UI guide — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A job joins a large events table with a small users table on `account_id`, and a handful of accounts hold most of the rows. The Spark UI shows one straggler task per run, and AQE skew handling never triggers because the oversized partition stays below both size thresholds. Which technique redistributes the hot key manually?
options: Increase `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` far above the current value, so that the single hot key's rows spread across many smaller tasks
Broadcast the large events table to every executor, so each task joins its local slice against the users table
Append a random salt value (0 to N) to `account_id`, replicate each users row across every salt, and join on the composite key
Repartition the events table by `account_id` before the join, so all rows of each key are co-located in one partition
snapshot.referenceTitle: Investigate long-running stages in the Spark UI — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A nightly aggregation shuffles about 6 GB of data. The plan submitted to the cluster ended with 200 post-shuffle partitions, yet the Spark UI shows the final stage ran only 12 tasks, each processing a reasonably sized slice — and nobody edited the query. Which mechanism changed the task count while the query was running?
options: The driver, which locks the final task count when the plan is compiled and submitted for execution
Adaptive Query Execution, which coalesces small post-shuffle partitions into fewer, larger tasks using runtime statistics
A manual repartition transformation, which engineers are required to add to every job before Spark can merge its small shuffle partitions
Photon, whose vectorized engine merges small partitions while it executes the stage's scans and aggregations
snapshot.referenceTitle: Adaptive Query Execution — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A PySpark job reads a large Delta table that was written as many small files. The read stage schedules over 4,000 tasks that each finish in a fraction of a second, and most of the stage time goes to scheduling overhead. Which setting controls how much data each read task processes, so the small files can be packed into fewer tasks?
options: `spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes`, which however only influences the size of the files written by the job's outputs
The cluster's core count, because input splits are derived solely from the number of worker nodes and no tunable target size exists
The split target, which must never be raised, because larger tasks always degrade reads in every workload
`spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes`, which sets how many bytes are packed into a single read partition (128 MB by default)
snapshot.referenceTitle: Spark UI guide — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A sales fact table is partitioned by `order_date`. A query filters `WHERE order_date = '2026-10-02'`, but it still scans hundreds of gigabytes and runs for minutes. Before touching the table, the engineer wants to confirm whether the partition filter was actually applied to the scan. How can the engineer verify this in the query plan?
options: Run the query and inspect the Ganglia charts afterward, the only place where partition pruning statistics are exposed
Accept that pruning is an internal optimizer step that never becomes visible in any plan output
Run EXPLAIN, or open the plan in the query profile, and check the scan node for the partition predicates applied
Skip the check, because partition pruning applies automatically to filters on any column of the table
snapshot.referenceTitle: Spark UI guide — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A data engineer supports dozens of Databricks SQL users and keeps finding the same performance problems: tables fragmented into small files, exploding joins, and skewed aggregations. The engineer wants a place where the platform itself flags these issues for specific queries and suggests what to do about them. Where should the engineer look?
options: Performance insights, which appear in query history and the query profile with actionable recommendations
Databricks Support tickets, because query recommendations are authored only by the support team on request
The insights page, which makes modeling decisions like schema and partitioning choices on the engineer's behalf
Cached query results, the only executions for which the platform generates performance insight recommendations
snapshot.referenceTitle: Query performance insights — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: In the jobs timeline, one stage of a nightly Lakeflow Job takes 40 minutes while its sibling stages finish in about three minutes each. Before changing any configuration, the engineer wants to understand why this particular stage is slow. What is the recommended next step in the investigation?
options: Resize the cluster to a larger and more expensive node type right away, since a long stage always means the hardware is undersized
Open the stage page and examine the task duration distribution, summary metrics for skew, and spill statistics
Assume the notebook code has a bug, because stages only run long when user code contains an error
Cancel and resubmit the run, because re-execution is the documented way to clear a long-running stage
snapshot.referenceTitle: Investigate long-running stages in the Spark UI — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A complex batch ETL join stage spills over 40 GB of shuffle data to local disk on every nightly run. The query cannot be redesigned this quarter, so the team wants a compute-level change that reduces the spill without touching the code. Which change follows the documented guidance?
options: Treat the spill as harmless log noise, because writing shuffle data to disk never slows a stage down
Reduce the memory per executor, which forces Spark to launch more tasks and split the shuffle data among them
Disable Adaptive Query Execution, which removes partition coalescing and with it all spill from the stage
Use instances with more memory, or fewer and larger workers, so more of the shuffle fits before spilling
snapshot.referenceTitle: Spark UI guide — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A team changed one shuffle configuration on their nightly pipeline, and the on-call engineer reports that the job 'feels faster' now. Before rolling the change out to the other pipelines, the lead wants proof that the tuning actually improved the slow stage. What is the correct way to verify it?
options: Run the same workload before and after the change, then compare stage duration and spill in the Spark UI
Change several more tuning parameters at once, then judge the combined effect on the pipeline's total runtime
Trust the on-call engineer's impression, because perceived runtime is a reliable signal of pipeline performance
Compare Git commit timestamps around the change, which serve as a proxy for how long each pipeline run took
snapshot.referenceTitle: Spark UI guide — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A pro SQL warehouse serves the company's morning dashboards. At 9 a.m., more concurrent queries arrive than the running clusters can execute, and analysts watch their queries sit in QUEUED status. The warehouse is configured with a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 6 clusters. What does the warehouse do while queries are queued?
options: It keeps them queued and provisions additional clusters of the same size, up to the configured maximum, to drain the backlog
It replaces each cluster's driver with a larger driver type, which frees capacity for every waiting query
It fails the queued queries immediately with a timeout, forcing analysts to resubmit after the morning peak
It keeps growing past the configured maximum, because warehouse scale-out has no configurable limit
snapshot.referenceTitle: SQL warehouse sizing, scaling, and queuing behavior — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A long-running job on a cluster with spot workers loses one mid-run: the node is reclaimed by the cloud provider, and a shuffle stage that had tasks on that node is suddenly incomplete. A new engineer assumes the whole job run is lost.

What actually happens?
options: Spark re-executes the lost tasks and dependent stages, so the run continues without starting over
The entire job run fails immediately, and Lakeflow Jobs restarts the whole thing from the first task
The lost tasks are skipped, so the run completes with silently missing partitions
Spot reclamation pauses the job until the same node type becomes available again
snapshot.referenceTitle: Configure clusters — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: An external security auditor is reviewing how the company's lakehouse reaches its cloud storage. The platform lead explains that one Unity Catalog object encapsulates the cloud credential — an AWS IAM role — that authorizes access to storage paths, and the auditor asks who in the platform can create that object. Which explanation is accurate?
options: Any lakehouse user can create a storage credential whenever they register a new cloud storage path for their team.
A storage credential is created at the metastore level by a metastore admin or a principal granted CREATE STORAGE CREDENTIAL.
Storage credentials live inside individual schemas, next to the tables and volumes that read from their storage paths.
Storage credentials are account-wide objects that every user shares automatically, with no Unity Catalog privilege required to use them.
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Unity Catalog? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A new analytics domain is joining the lakehouse, and the governance team plans to give it a dedicated Unity Catalog catalog so its schemas and tables stay separate from other domains. The platform admin who will create the catalog asks which privilege the task requires. Which answer is correct?
options: CREATE CATALOG on the metastore, a privilege that metastore and account admins can grant to other principals.
USE CATALOG on an existing catalog, since usage privileges on one catalog authorize creating sibling catalogs.
Workspace admin in every workspace attached to the metastore, because catalog creation is a workspace-scoped operation.
SELECT on at least one existing catalog, because demonstrated read access is the prerequisite for creating new catalogs.
snapshot.referenceTitle: Manage privileges in Unity Catalog — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A data engineer created the Unity Catalog table main.finance.risk_scores and owned it until she changed teams. No GRANT statement ever named her user, yet she could always query the table, modify its data, and grant other groups access to it. Her successor asks how that was possible. What is the explanation?
options: Object owners receive hidden grants that SHOW GRANTS deliberately omits from its output to keep listings short.
An owner's only automatic capability is dropping the table; reads and writes still require explicitly granted privileges.
Unity Catalog grants owners every capability on their object implicitly — including granting privileges to other principals.
Ownership cannot be transferred after creation, so the engineer's account must keep owning the table forever.
snapshot.referenceTitle: Manage privileges in Unity Catalog — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
A governance program is rolling out governed tags — key-value classifications such as pii=high — so that ABAC policies can act on them uniformly. The data governance lead is documenting where these tags are defined and who can create them.

Which statement matches the platform?
options: Governed tags are defined per metastore, and any metastore admin can create them freely
Governed tags are created ad hoc by users on their own tables, with no central control
Governed tags are account-level, applying across the whole estate including multiple metastores
Governed tags are defined per workspace and never shared between workspaces
snapshot.referenceTitle: Attribute-based access control — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: The governance team plans to rename msrp, a single column in main.products.price_list, a 60-column table with dozens of downstream dashboards and pipelines. Most consumers never touch that column, so the team wants to reach only the assets that actually depend on it, instead of every consumer of the table. Which Unity Catalog capability supports this?
options: Unity Catalog tracks lineage at the table level only, so every consumer of the table counts as affected.
Unity Catalog captures lineage down to the column level, and Catalog Explorer shows which assets depend on that column.
Column lineage becomes available only after an administrator enables audit logging on each table that needs tracking.
Column-level lineage is captured only for external tables, because their files live outside the managed storage location.
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Unity Catalog? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A platform team is designing file storage under Unity Catalog. Machine learning artifacts produced by Databricks jobs should live in storage that Unity Catalog fully controls, including deletion. A large reference dataset already sits in a bucket owned by another application, must stay there, and must never be deleted by Databricks. How should the team create the two volumes?
options: Create both as external volumes, because Unity Catalog volumes must always reference paths governed by an external location.
Create both as managed volumes, each with an explicit LOCATION clause that names its destination storage path.
Create a managed volume for the artifacts and an external volume with LOCATION for the reference dataset.
Create an external volume for the artifacts so that dropping it purges their files, and a managed volume for the reference dataset.
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Unity Catalog? — Databricks Docs

options: They lose SELECT on every table under main at once, because those reads were inherited from the catalog-level grant.
They keep reading the tables, because the surviving USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA privileges are what authorize data access.
Their access persists until an administrator repeats the REVOKE on every schema and every table under main.
The REVOKE is ignored below the catalog, because Unity Catalog copies inherited privileges into each table when granting them.
snapshot.referenceTitle: Manage privileges in Unity Catalog — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: During a security architecture review, the team is documenting every kind of object that Unity Catalog can protect with grants, beyond the familiar catalogs, schemas, and tables. The reviewer asks which other object types are securables that carry their own privilege types. Which answer is accurate?
options: Only tables are securables; every other object is protected indirectly through the privileges of the catalog that contains it.
Views, volumes, and functions exist as governed objects, but none of them carries privileges of its own.
Storage credentials and external locations are cloud-side constructs that Unity Catalog references but cannot govern.
Views, volumes, functions, external locations, storage credentials, and connections are all securables with their own privileges.
snapshot.referenceTitle: Manage privileges in Unity Catalog — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
Five workspaces share one Unity Catalog metastore, and by default every workspace can see every catalog. A new compliance requirement says one analytics catalog may be exposed to only two of the five workspaces, without splitting it into separate copies.

Which mechanism implements this?
options: Create a second metastore and replicate the whole catalog into it for the other workspaces
Grant USE CATALOG to the analysts group and rely on group membership per workspace
Convert the catalog's tables to external tables stored in a separate storage account
Workspace-catalog binding: assign the catalog to a restricted list of workspaces
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Unity Catalog? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: Security policy requires rotating the AWS IAM role that backs the company's lakehouse storage every quarter. The role is attached to a Unity Catalog storage credential that several external locations and external tables depend on. The platform team must implement the rotation without recreating objects or interrupting nightly pipelines. Which approach meets the requirement?
options: Create a second storage credential, then drop and recreate every external location and table against it during a release window.
Update the existing storage credential with the new IAM role, so external locations and tables keep referencing the same object.
Pause all pipelines during a maintenance window, rotate the role in AWS, and wait for Unity Catalog to rediscover the credential.
Create a new storage credential every quarter, because credentials are immutable once an external location references them.
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Unity Catalog? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A platform team keeps its production notebooks in a Databricks Git folder cloned from the team's GitHub repository. External auditors must be allowed to open and read the folder's notebooks and run them on sample data, but they must not edit files, create branches, or push changes. How should a workspace admin grant the auditors' group this access?
options: Grant the auditors CAN RUN on the Git folder: workspace objects like Git folders use their own permission levels (CAN READ, CAN RUN, CAN EDIT, CAN MANAGE).
Grant the auditors SELECT on the Git folder through Unity Catalog, because Git folders are securables governed by the metastore like tables.
Grant the auditors nothing on the folder, because every workspace user can already view, edit, and run any Git folder by default.
Grant the auditors CAN RUN on the catalog's Delta tables, because permissions on a Git folder automatically extend to the data its notebooks read.
snapshot.referenceTitle: Git folders concepts — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A production pipeline reads its database password from the Databricks secret scope etl-secrets. The analysts' group must be able to read an API key stored in that same scope, but the group must not be allowed to change the scope's access rules or overwrite secret values. How should the admin grant the analysts this access?
options: Grant nothing on the scope, because any workspace user can already read the secrets stored in every secret scope by default.
Grant the group SELECT on the secret scope through Unity Catalog, because secret scope ACLs are inherited automatically from Unity Catalog group privileges.
Grant the group the READ permission on the scope's ACL: READ allows reading secret values, and only MANAGE can change the scope's permissions.
Grant the group MANAGE on the scope, because MANAGE is the permission level that lets principals read secret values.
snapshot.referenceTitle: Manage secrets — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A contractor's engagement ends today, and the offboarding checklist requires that all access to Unity Catalog data be cut off before the end of the day. An access review confirms that the contractor's privileges on dozens of tables all arrive through membership in three groups; the contractor holds no direct grants. Which action cuts off the contractor's data access completely and verifiably?
options: Revoke SELECT from each of the three groups on every table they can currently read, working through the dozens of objects one by one before the end of the day.
Wait for the contractor's personal access tokens to expire, which automatically disables the account's data access.
Rename the contractor's user account so that sign-in fails, and leave the group memberships and all grants exactly as they are.
Remove the contractor from the three groups: every privilege arrived through membership, so this single change cuts off all table access and is auditable.
snapshot.referenceTitle: Manage privileges in Unity Catalog — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A global company syncs its Databricks groups from its identity provider using automatic identity management. The group data-latam is a nested member of the corporate group data-global, which holds SELECT on the catalog analytics. A data engineer whose only group is data-latam runs a query against a table in analytics. What happens?
options: The query fails: Databricks groups cannot be nested, so data-latam would have to be flattened into data-global before any grant can apply.
The query succeeds: members of nested groups inherit the parent's permissions, so the SELECT granted to data-global applies to data-latam's members.
The query fails: privileges granted to a group apply only to the users and service principals listed as its direct members.
The query succeeds, but only because Unity Catalog automatically duplicates the parent's grant onto every child group at the moment the nesting is created.
snapshot.referenceTitle: Manage privileges in Unity Catalog — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
Finance needs a monthly cost breakdown of Databricks usage by team for chargeback, computed from the lakehouse itself rather than from invoices or the cloud provider's console.

Which approach meets this?
options: Query system.billing.usage, filtering by workspace and tags, aggregating DBUs and dollars per team
Parse the monthly PDF invoices with a notebook and load the results into a Delta table
Read the cloud provider's billing export, which already itemizes Databricks DBUs per team and workspace
Enable a workspace setting that emails each team leader their DBU total every month
snapshot.referenceTitle: System tables reference — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A company runs one Unity Catalog metastore shared by several business domains. Security policy requires that every managed table created in the finance catalog keeps its data files under a storage prefix dedicated to finance (s3://acme-managed/finance/), instead of the metastore root storage used by other domains. How should the platform team configure this?
options: Spin up a second metastore whose root storage is the finance prefix, because managed storage locations exist only at the metastore level.
Leave the catalog as it is, because managed tables in every catalog are always written to the metastore's root storage location and can never use anything else.
Create the finance catalog with MANAGED LOCATION 's3://acme-managed/finance/', overriding the metastore root storage for that catalog's managed tables.
Create the finance tables as external tables with LOCATION under the finance prefix, because managed locations per catalog work only with external tables.
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Unity Catalog? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: During an architecture review, a new data engineer must explain how three Unity Catalog objects work together for cloud storage: the object that holds the IAM credential, the object that registers a storage path for external tables, and the object that gives notebooks governed access to files. Which explanation is correct?
options: Volumes have replaced external locations entirely, so a single volume type now covers both the registration of storage paths for tables and practical access to files.
Storage credentials point to the catalogs that use them and carry the privilege to run queries against those catalogs.
External locations store the IAM credentials of every external table registered under them, one credential per table.
Storage credentials hold the IAM credential, external locations register a storage path referencing it, and volumes give governed access to files.
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Unity Catalog? — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: A Lakeflow Job writes manifest files directly to the cloud storage path s3://acme-dropzone/manifests/, which is registered in Unity Catalog as the external location acme_dropzone. The job runs under the service principal loader-sp and does not write through any table or volume. Which grant authorizes the job's writes?
options: Grant the service principal WRITE FILES on the external location acme_dropzone, which authorizes direct writes on the registered path.
Grant the service principal SELECT on the external location acme_dropzone, which is the standard read privilege for governed data objects.
Grant the service principal WRITE VOLUME on the external location acme_dropzone, because volume privileges cover its registered storage paths.
Grant the service principal nothing, because Unity Catalog cannot authorize direct writes to a storage path outside tables and volumes.
snapshot.referenceTitle: Manage privileges in Unity Catalog — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement: During a security review, an auditor asks what the Databricks audit trail actually captures, expecting it to log only SQL queries. The platform lead must answer based on the documented coverage of the audit log system table (system.access.audit). Which answer is accurate?
options: Only SELECT statements are captured; every other kind of event, including permission changes and object creation, is out of the audit trail's scope.
Only sign-in events are captured; queries run against the lakehouse are recorded solely in query history, never in audit logs.
A broad range of events is captured: logins and logouts, queries, permission changes such as grants, and object changes, each with the acting principal and timestamp.
Permission changes are not captured; audit events record queries and logins but never grants or revokes on governed objects.
snapshot.referenceTitle: Audit log system table reference — Databricks Docs

snapshot.statement:
An IT director at a logistics company is preparing the team's first Azure project. During the kickoff meeting, a project manager asks for a plain-language definition of cloud computing.

Which statement should the IT director give?
options: A model in which you buy physical servers up front and house them in the company's own datacenter
The delivery of computing services over the internet, including virtual machines, storage, databases, and networking
A way of delivering computing services over the company's private internal network, with no external provider involved
An arrangement where a vendor builds and operates a datacenter on the company's premises and bills a fixed annual fee
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is cloud computing — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
A training nonprofit is onboarding a new cloud analyst. As a first exercise, the analyst lists what counts as a cloud computing service.

Which list is accurate?
options: Virtual machines, storage, databases, and networking, plus newer offerings such as Internet of Things, machine learning, and AI
Only the physical hardware layer: the compute racks, power, and cooling that providers operate in their regions
Only ready-to-use business applications, such as email and customer relationship management tools
Only hosting plans for public websites, of the kind providers resell to small businesses
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is cloud computing — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
A streaming service is producing an interactive live event that will multiply its normal traffic for a few days; after the event, demand returns to its usual level. The team wants extra capacity for those days without waiting to build new datacenter capacity.

Which statement describes how cloud computing supports this?
options: The team must buy enough hardware up front to cover the event's peak and keep it available for the rest of the year
The team uses the cloud to rapidly expand its IT footprint for the event and scale back down afterward, without building a new datacenter
The team's IT footprint stays constrained by the physical infrastructure of its own datacenter
The team rents a dedicated datacenter for a full year even though the extra capacity is needed for only a few days
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is cloud computing — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
A flower delivery company sees orders multiply around Valentine's Day and Mother's Day. In past years, preparing for those peaks meant long procurement cycles for servers, and much of that equipment sat idle between peaks.

At a fundamentals level, how does cloud computing change this planning?
options: Planning still starts with long procurement cycles, but the provider finances the hardware purchases for the company
Planning is handled by the provider, which forecasts the company's demand and provisions capacity on its behalf
Planning becomes a single up-front decision: buy capacity for the highest expected peak and keep it running year-round
Planning shifts from long procurement cycles to on-demand provisioning: capacity is added for the peak and released afterward
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is cloud computing — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
A hospital network is moving its workloads to the cloud. A compliance officer asks which responsibilities always remain with the cloud provider, regardless of the service type the hospital uses.

Which statement is accurate?
options: The information and data stored in the cloud, and the accounts that use the services
The physical datacenter, the physical network, the physical hosts, and the underlying infrastructure
The operating systems and the network controls, whichever service type is used
The applications and the devices allowed to connect to the cloud
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe the shared responsibility model — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
A retailer has adopted a public cloud. A newly hired security engineer is reviewing what the company must keep doing itself, no matter which cloud service type it adopts.

Which responsibilities always stay with the retailer?
options: The physical hosts, the physical network, and the underlying infrastructure that run its workloads in the provider's datacenter
The operating systems, the network controls, and the applications, whichever service type the retailer adopts
The power, the cooling, and the physical security of the datacenter where its workloads run
The data in the cloud, the devices allowed to connect, and the accounts and identities in the environment
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe the shared responsibility model — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
An external auditor is comparing the company's former on-premises datacenter with its current public cloud setup, and asks how responsibilities shifted when the workloads moved.

Which statement is accurate?
options: On-premises, the company handled everything; in the cloud, physical security, power, cooling, and connectivity moved to the provider
On-premises, the provider handled physical security; in the cloud, the company became responsible for everything
Moving to the cloud transferred responsibility for the stored data and for access security over to the provider
Moving to the cloud made the provider responsible for patching the company's applications in every service type
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe the shared responsibility model — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
A manufacturing company's cloud architect is briefing the infrastructure team on how the shared responsibility model behaves across service types, ahead of the team's first migration wave.

Which statement is accurate?
options: SaaS places the most responsibility on the consumer, while IaaS shifts nearly everything to the cloud provider
All three service types split responsibilities identically between the provider and the consumer, whatever the workload demands
IaaS places the most responsibility on the consumer, SaaS on the provider, and PaaS splits responsibility between the two
The service type has no bearing on who maintains the operating systems and the applications running in the cloud
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe the shared responsibility model — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A fintech runs two database workloads in the cloud. One is a SQL database that the team installed on its own virtual machines and patches itself. The other is a managed cloud SQL database service. Under the shared responsibility model, who maintains each database engine?
options: The provider maintains both engines, because all database software running in the cloud is managed by the provider
The fintech maintains the engine on its virtual machines; the provider maintains the managed cloud SQL database
The fintech maintains both engines, because anything database-related always stays with the consumer
The provider maintains both engines, though the fintech stays responsible for the data in each case
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe the shared responsibility model — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
A university is evaluating its first cloud deployment, and a lecturer on the evaluation committee asks what a public cloud is.

Which statement is accurate?
options: A cloud used by a single entity, with resources dedicated to one organization and no other tenants sharing them
A cloud that combines the university's on-premises datacenter with a provider's cloud in an interconnected environment
A cloud operated jointly by two providers, in which workloads can move freely between the providers' platforms
A cloud built, controlled, and maintained by a third-party provider, where anyone can purchase cloud services and use them
snapshot.referenceTitle: Define cloud models — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
A pharmaceutical company wants cloud technology, but its resources must be dedicated to the organization alone. A team member asks what a private cloud is.

Which statement is accurate?
options: A cloud environment used by a single entity, hosted on-site or in a dedicated offsite datacenter, even a third-party one
A cloud where anyone can purchase access and where resources are shared with other tenants in the provider's own datacenter
A temporary public deployment used to handle surges in demand on top of the organization's own datacenter
A cloud model in which two public providers jointly run the environment as if it were a single cloud
snapshot.referenceTitle: Define cloud models — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
An insurance company keeps a private cloud in its own datacenter and connects it to a public cloud so it can absorb temporary demand spikes without changing its steady-state setup.

Which statement about this environment is accurate?
options: It is two public clouds, from different providers, operated as one interconnected environment, with the private datacenter retired
It is a public cloud in which the provider dedicates hardware to a single tenant inside its own datacenter
It is a private cloud whose spare resources are shared with other tenants during peak periods to absorb the demand spikes
It is a hybrid cloud: interconnected public and private clouds, where the private side surges for temporary demand using public resources
snapshot.referenceTitle: Define cloud models — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
A gaming studio uses one public provider for its development platform and is moving part of its workloads to a second public provider to use features the first one lacks, while the migration is still in progress.

Which statement describes this environment accurately?
options: It is a hybrid cloud scenario, because the studio is combining two different cloud models into one
It is a multicloud scenario: the studio uses two public cloud providers and manages resources and security in both environments
It is a private cloud scenario, because each provider dedicates its environment to the studio alone
It is still a single public cloud scenario, because using several public providers at once does not change the model
snapshot.referenceTitle: Define cloud models — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
