A solutions architect is preparing a briefing that compares cloud models for a client's board. One slide pairs characteristics with the models, and the architect checks it before the meeting.

Which pairing is accurate?
options: Private cloud: no capital expenditures to scale up, because the provider pays for the hardware
Hybrid cloud: you have complete control over resources and security at all times
Public cloud: no capital expenditures to scale up — you pay only for what you use
Public cloud: your data isn't collocated with other tenants' data
snapshot.referenceTitle: Define cloud models — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
During a proposal review, a client asks the architect to confirm which statement about cloud models is accurate before it goes into the final deck.

Which statement is it?
options: In a private cloud, hardware must be purchased for startup and maintenance, and the organization maintains and updates it
In a public cloud, the consumer purchases and maintains the hardware that runs the services in the provider's datacenter
In a hybrid cloud, the provider decides where each application runs, based on cost optimization
In a multicloud environment, the security policies of one provider automatically govern the other provider's resources
snapshot.referenceTitle: Define cloud models — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
A defense contractor must run all of its workloads on dedicated infrastructure that the organization controls. Its data cannot be collocated with other tenants' data, and it will not use any public cloud resources for these workloads.

Which cloud model fits these requirements?
options: Public cloud, because dedicated hardware can be reserved in public regions for use by a single tenant
Hybrid cloud, because the sensitive workloads stay on the private side of the environment
Private cloud, because resources are dedicated to one entity and data isn't collocated with other tenants' data
Multicloud, because spreading the workloads across two public providers isolates them from other tenants
snapshot.referenceTitle: Define cloud models — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
Two founders are building a mobile app with no capital to buy servers. Usage is expected to grow unpredictably if the app takes off. They want to pay only for what they use, provision and deprovision applications quickly, and avoid managing resources in multiple environments.

Which cloud model fits best?
options: Public cloud: no capital expenditures to scale up, quick provisioning, and you pay only for what you use
Private cloud: hardware purchased up front for startup and maintenance, in exchange for complete control over resources and security
Hybrid cloud: start in a connected on-premises datacenter and add public capacity later when demand grows
Multicloud: split the app across two public providers from day one, to spread the load
snapshot.referenceTitle: Define cloud models — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
A tax-preparation firm runs a private cloud that carries a steady load for most of the year. During filing season, demand rises sharply for a few weeks. The firm wants to keep its steady-state workloads where they are and temporarily deploy extra capacity from a public cloud, connected to its own environment.

Which approach does this describe?
options: Public cloud: migrating the whole private environment to the provider for the season and keeping it there
Private cloud: buying additional hardware for the peak and keeping it available for the rest of the year
Multicloud: renting extra capacity from a second public provider during the season, alongside the first
Hybrid cloud: letting the private cloud surge for increased, temporary demand by deploying public cloud resources
snapshot.referenceTitle: Define cloud models — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
An energy utility uses one public provider for its customer portal and a second public provider for analytics, because each offers features the other lacks; the migration between them is still in progress.

Beyond naming the model, what does operating this environment require?
options: Extending one provider's security policies automatically across the other provider's resources
Managing resources and security in both public cloud environments
Consolidating both providers into a single public cloud before management becomes possible
Managing only the environment that hosts the newest workloads
snapshot.referenceTitle: Define cloud models — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:

Azure App Service
Azure Virtual Desktop

options: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), which manages the lifecycle of a fleet of containers
Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets, which run the job across automatically scaled virtual machine instances
Azure App Service, which hosts the container behind a managed web endpoint
Azure Container Instances, which runs a single container without managing virtual machines or adopting a higher-level service

Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), the managed Kubernetes service that runs the control plane for the company

An Azure DNS zone shared by both virtual networks

Azure Data Box uploads files to Azure over the customer's internet connection while the device is on site
snapshot.referenceTitle: Identify Azure file movement options — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A public sector agency plans to move its on-premises datacenter — servers, databases, and web applications — to Azure. Leadership wants a central place to assess readiness and hosting costs before deciding, and then run the migration with minimal downtime. Which service should they use?
options: Azure Data Box, which ships a physical appliance to the customer to transfer bulk data into Azure
Azure File Sync, which extends on-premises file servers into Azure file shares
Azure Migrate, a central hub for assessing and migrating on-premises servers, databases, and apps to Azure
AzCopy, which copies server disks into storage accounts over the network
snapshot.referenceTitle: About Azure Migrate — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A film studio must move tens of terabytes of raw footage into Azure before an archive deadline. The studio's internet connection is too slow to transfer the data over the network within the available window. Which option is designed for this situation?
options: AzCopy, running continuously over the studio's existing internet connection until the whole transfer completes
Azure Migrate, which transfers large media archives to Azure over an accelerated network link
Azure File Sync, which uploads the footage to Azure in the background as it is edited
Azure Data Box, a physical migration service where a shipped device is loaded locally and returned for upload
snapshot.referenceTitle: Microsoft Azure Data Box overview — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: An IT administrator at a research institute has just taken delivery of an Azure Data Box device at the loading dock. Which sequence describes how the import process works, from setup to upload?
options: Microsoft permanently installs the device in the datacenter as an on-premises edge cache for Azure Storage
The administrator copies data onto the device, which uploads it to Azure over the internet while it is on site
The administrator ships the institute's own storage disks to Microsoft, which loads the data into a storage account
The device is set up through its local web UI, loaded on site, and returned; Microsoft uploads the data to Azure
snapshot.referenceTitle: Identify Azure data migration options — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: During a datacenter exit, a grocery chain must accomplish two things: evaluate which on-premises servers are ready for Azure and migrate them with minimal downtime, and move an archive of tens of terabytes of historical sales data over a slow WAN link within a fixed window. Which combination of services should they use?
options: Azure Data Box for both, because it also assesses server readiness before the data is shipped
Azure Migrate for both, because its online data transfers are unaffected by the slow WAN link
Azure Migrate to assess and migrate the servers, and Azure Data Box to move the archive
AzCopy and Azure File Sync, which together provide server assessment and physical data transfer
snapshot.referenceTitle: Identify Azure data migration options — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
A regional hospital network is moving its email, collaboration tools, and several custom web apps to the cloud. The IT director wants a single cloud service that manages employee identities and lets each employee sign in with one account to reach Microsoft 365 and the custom apps.
Which Azure service should the director choose?
options: Microsoft Entra Domain Services, which runs managed domain controllers for applications that need classic AD DS
Azure Firewall, which filters network traffic between the hospital's apps and the internet
Microsoft Entra ID, the cloud-based identity and access management service for Microsoft and custom cloud applications
Microsoft Purview, which governs and classifies the hospital's data estate
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe Azure directory services — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
An industrial-equipment manufacturer runs a legacy inventory application that authenticates users with NTLM and needs its servers to be domain-joined. The company is moving the application to Azure and wants to retire its on-premises domain controllers entirely, with no configuring, patching, or monitoring of domain controllers by its own staff.
Which approach meets these requirements?
options: Deploy two Windows Server virtual machines as domain controllers and run them yourself in Azure
Create a Microsoft Entra Domain Services managed domain, in which Microsoft runs the domain controllers
Use Microsoft Entra ID alone, since it provides NTLM authentication and domain join for the application
Keep the on-premises domain controllers and extend them to Azure with a site-to-site VPN
snapshot.referenceTitle: Overview of Microsoft Entra Domain Services — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
A grocery chain uses a Microsoft Entra Domain Services managed domain so that a legacy warehouse application can keep using Kerberos and domain join. A newly hired identity administrator asks how employee identities relate to the managed domain: where the accounts live and how they reach the managed domain.
Which response is accurate?
options: The managed domain synchronizes two ways with Microsoft Entra ID, so changes made in either directory appear in both
The managed domain keeps its own user accounts, and employees receive separate credentials for domain-joined machines
The managed domain pulls accounts directly from an on-premises Active Directory forest, bypassing Microsoft Entra ID
The managed domain is fed by a one-way synchronization from Microsoft Entra ID, the source of authority for identities
snapshot.referenceTitle: Overview of Microsoft Entra Domain Services — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
During onboarding at a public-sector agency, a junior cloud architect is asked to summarize, in one sentence, how Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft Entra Domain Services divide the work in Azure.
Which statement is accurate?
options: Microsoft Entra Domain Services provides managed domain services (domain join, group policy, LDAP, Kerberos/NTLM authentication) without any domain controllers to manage
Microsoft Entra ID provides domain join, group policy, LDAP, and Kerberos/NTLM authentication for legacy line-of-business applications
Microsoft Entra Domain Services is the identity service that employees use to sign in to Microsoft 365, SaaS applications, and the company's own custom cloud applications
Microsoft Entra Domain Services requires you to deploy, patch, and monitor your own Windows Server domain controllers in Azure
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe Azure directory services — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
At a logistics company, warehouse staff must sign in separately to the route-planning app, the inventory app, and Microsoft 365, and the help desk handles a constant stream of password resets. The IT lead wants employees to sign in once with one set of credentials and then open every assigned app without signing in again.
Which capability should the IT lead enable?
options: Multifactor authentication, prompting each user for an additional verification factor during the sign-in process
Passwordless sign-in, replacing passwords with Windows Hello or a FIDO2 security key
Single sign-on, which lets users sign in once and reach every assigned application
Conditional Access policies, blocking or challenging sign-ins that come from unexpected locations
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is single sign-on in Microsoft Entra ID? — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
A payments company suffered a phishing incident in which attackers captured employees' passwords. The security team now requires each sign-in to demand more than a password: after entering the password, each employee must approve the request on their registered phone before access is granted.
Which approach does the team require at sign-in?
options: Multifactor authentication, combining something the employee knows with something the employee has
Single sign-on, using one trusted authentication to cover every application
Passwordless authentication, replacing the password with a biometric or a hardware security key
Longer passwords rotated more frequently, so that a stolen password becomes obsolete quickly
snapshot.referenceTitle: Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication overview — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
A hotel chain's IT team spends too much effort on password resets, and auditors flag password reuse across properties. The team decides to remove passwords from the sign-in experience altogether: staff will sign in with a biometric or a PIN tied to their own Windows PC, with a tap of a FIDO2 security key, or with a number match in the Microsoft Authenticator app.
Which approach is the team adopting?
options: Multifactor authentication, which adds an extra verification factor on top of the user's password at sign-in
Single sign-on, which lets one authentication cover all of the chain's applications
Conditional Access, which requires a second factor only for sign-ins from unexpected locations
Passwordless authentication, which eliminates passwords with Windows Hello for Business, Authenticator, or FIDO2 security keys
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe Azure authentication methods — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
A junior security analyst at a media company is writing study notes about the authentication methods available in Microsoft Entra ID. The notes must state precisely what single sign-on, multifactor authentication, and passwordless sign-in each do.
Which statement should the notes contain?
options: Single sign-on requires a hardware key at every sign-in; multifactor authentication covers one application at a time; passwordless still asks for the password on untrusted devices
Single sign-on lets a user sign in once and access multiple applications; multifactor authentication requires credentials from more than one category; passwordless methods eliminate the password
Single sign-on eliminates the password; multifactor authentication signs users in with no credential at all; passwordless adds a second factor to the password
Single sign-on applies to Microsoft apps only; multifactor authentication replaces passwords with biometrics; passwordless rotates passwords automatically
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe Azure authentication methods — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
A utility company requires multifactor authentication for remote access to its control-room dashboard. A dispatcher signs in with her password and then approves the request on her phone, which is registered as her verification method.
Which two categories of credentials has the dispatcher presented?
options: Something you know and something you are
Something you have and something you are
Something you know and something you have
Something you are, because the phone is unlocked with a fingerprint
snapshot.referenceTitle: Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication overview — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
A university runs a joint research program with an engineering firm. About 40 of the firm's engineers need access to a few of the university's web apps for the semester. The firm manages its own identities, and its engineers must keep using their existing work accounts rather than new credentials. The university must stay in control of which apps the guests can reach.
Which approach should the university use?
options: Create a local account in the university's tenant for each engineer, with new passwords issued by the university
Invite the engineers as guest users through Microsoft Entra B2B collaboration, so they sign in with their own work identities
Set up B2B direct connect with the firm's tenant, so the engineers can reach the university's web apps from their home tenant
Use External ID for customers, so the engineers sign up for the university's apps with social identities
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Microsoft Entra B2B collaboration? — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
An environmental nonprofit invites staff from a partner agency to collaborate on its Microsoft 365 environment. The invited users have just redeemed their invitations.
What does the nonprofit's administrator now see in the nonprofit's own directory?
options: Guest user objects representing the partners, who sign in with their own work, school, or social identities
Nothing; invited users remain invisible until they register new credentials in the nonprofit's tenant
Full employee accounts with temporary passwords that the nonprofit must reset at first sign-in
A read-only replica of the partner agency's entire home directory, synchronized into the nonprofit's tenant
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Microsoft Entra B2B collaboration? — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
An automotive supplier onboarding a new parts partner asks its security lead to explain, for the kickoff deck, how external identities work in Azure. Both companies already use Microsoft 365 for day-to-day collaboration.
Which statement is accurate?
options: External users must be issued accounts with passwords in the supplier's tenant before they can access any resource
B2B collaboration requires partners to run Microsoft Entra ID on their side
External identities let outsiders access approved resources with their existing credentials, while the organization controls what they reach
External identities give partner users the same access to resources as the supplier's own employees
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe Azure external identities — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
A streaming service wants a consistent rule for its Microsoft 365 apps: employees signing in from the office or other known locations proceed normally, but a sign-in from an unexpected location must be challenged for a second factor before access is granted.
Which Microsoft Entra capability should the security team configure?
options: Azure role-based access control, assigning the Contributor role at the subscription scope
Multifactor authentication enforced for every user on every sign-in, regardless of location
Azure Policy, blocking the deployment of any resources that do not match its compliance rules
Microsoft Entra Conditional Access, which evaluates sign-in signals and enforces decisions such as requiring MFA
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe Azure conditional access — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
An identity architect at a software company is sketching how Microsoft Entra Conditional Access works for a design review. The sketch has two boxes: one for the signals a policy can evaluate, one for the decisions it can enforce.
Which list is accurate?
options: Signals — allow access, require multifactor authentication, block access; decisions — user or group, IP location, device in use, application, sign-in risk
Signals — virtual machine size, storage tier, and region; decisions — allow access, possibly requiring multifactor authentication, or block access
Signals — user or group, IP location, device in use, application, sign-in risk; decisions — create a resource group, assign the Reader role, delete a subscription
Signals — user or group, IP location, device in use, application, sign-in risk; decisions — allow access, possibly requiring multifactor authentication, or block access
snapshot.referenceTitle: Microsoft Entra Conditional Access: Zero Trust Policy Engine — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
During a design review at an e-commerce company, a newly hired architect keeps mixing up Conditional Access with Azure RBAC and Azure Policy.
Which statement would correctly describe Conditional Access?
options: Conditional Access policies grant users permissions to create and manage Azure resources, such as virtual machines, storage accounts, and virtual networks
Azure RBAC role assignments are evaluated at sign-in and challenge users for a second factor before granting resource access
Conditional Access policies evaluate identity signals, such as user, location, and device, and can allow access, require MFA, or block
Conditional Access policies enforce tagging and allowed regions on resources, updating the rules after those resources are deployed
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe Azure conditional access — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
A SaaS company with several engineering teams must control access to its Azure resources. Each team should receive only the level of access it needs to complete its tasks — no more — and that access should attach to a specific set of resources, such as one resource group.
Which mechanism should the company use?
options: Azure role-based access control, granting access through role assignments at a chosen scope
Microsoft Entra Conditional Access, evaluating identity signals at sign-in and challenging risky sign-ins
Azure Policy definitions, auditing and enforcing configuration rules on deployed resources
Resource locks, preventing the accidental deletion or modification of critical resources
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe Azure role-based access control — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
A game studio's deployment team must be able to create and manage all of the Azure resources in the studio's "game-builds" resource group. The studio's security policy adds one restriction: the team must not be able to grant other people access to those resources.
Which built-in role should the team be assigned at the resource group scope?
options: The Reader role, which grants access to view resources without allowing any changes
The Owner role, which grants full access to everything in the assigned scope
The User Access Administrator role, which lets the team manage user access to Azure resources
The Contributor role, which grants full access to manage all resources
snapshot.referenceTitle: Azure built-in roles — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
External auditors at a pharmaceutical company need to view every resource in one subscription — including resources in resource groups that will be created months from now — but they must not be able to change anything. The identity administrator wants a single role assignment that covers all of this automatically.
What should the administrator do?
options: Assign the Owner role to the auditors' group at the subscription scope, so that inheritance covers new resource groups
Assign the Reader role to the auditors' group at the subscription scope, so that inheritance covers every resource group and resource in the subscription
Assign the Reader role to the auditors' group separately in each existing resource group, repeating the assignment whenever a new resource group is created
Assign the Contributor role to the auditors' group at the management group scope, so that the whole hierarchy is covered
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe Azure role-based access control — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
A platform engineer is mentoring a newly hired Azure administrator on how role-based access control works. The administrator asks what a role assignment is made of and how permissions travel across the hierarchy.
Which statement should the engineer make?
options: Role definitions must be created individually for each user, so every user ends up with a custom role
Access granted at a child scope is inherited upward by parent scopes, so a role assigned in a resource group also applies at the subscription level
Every role assignment combines a security principal, a role definition, and a scope, and access granted at a parent scope is inherited by child scopes
Role assignments are enforced at application sign-in, where they can challenge the user for a second factor
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC)? — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
An insurance carrier's security office publishes a new access policy: always authenticate and authorize every request based on all available data, grant only just-enough access for the task at hand, and plan as if attackers are already inside the environment.
Which security model does this policy describe?
options: The Zero Trust model, built on verifying explicitly, using least privilege access, and assuming breach
The defense-in-depth model, built on a single hardened perimeter around the network
The shared responsibility model, splitting duties between the consumer and the cloud provider
The single sign-on model, letting one authentication reach many applications
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe Zero Trust model — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A field-services company lets technicians reach work apps from their own phones and home networks. Under the company's new Zero Trust policy, how is a sign-in like this one — from an unmanaged device on a public network — handled?
options: It is allowed without further checks, because it arrives through the company VPN tunnel from a known network
It is assessed on identity, device, and risk signals, then allowed, challenged for MFA, or blocked accordingly
It bypasses authentication whenever the target application is classified as low-risk, since trusted users are assumed safe
It is blocked outright, because Zero Trust only allows sign-ins from managed devices on the corporate network
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe Zero Trust model — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
A city government's IT architect presents the security design for a new records system: protections are stacked in multiple layers with the records at the center, and if an attacker gets through one layer, the later layers are still in place to slow the attack down and raise alerts.
Which security model is the architect describing?
options: The Zero Trust model
The defense-in-depth model
The shared responsibility model
The consumption-based model
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe defense-in-depth — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
While mapping controls for its defense-in-depth strategy, an airline's security team reaches the layer that directly protects customer records and operational data — the information the airline is ultimately trying to safeguard.
Which layer of the defense-in-depth model is this?
options: The application layer
The network layer
The data layer
The perimeter layer
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe defense-in-depth — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
A utility company runs workloads in Azure, in other clouds, and on on-premises servers. Its security team wants one tool that monitors the whole estate, continuously assesses its security posture, and provides recommendations and alerts to improve it.
Which service should the team use?
options: Microsoft Defender for Cloud, for security posture management and workload protection
Azure Monitor, for collecting and analyzing telemetry such as metrics and logs
Azure Advisor, for cost, performance, and reliability recommendations across subscriptions
Microsoft Purview, for data governance and classification across the data estate
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe Microsoft Defender for Cloud — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
The new CIO of a regional bank keeps mixing up the bank's security tools and asks the security lead for one accurate sentence about Microsoft Defender for Cloud.
Which statement is accurate?
options: It enforces resource tagging rules and allowed virtual machine sizes at deployment time, rejecting any resources that do not match those rules
It collects and analyzes application performance telemetry, such as request rates, failure counts, and page load times
It manages employee identities and single sign-on for the bank's cloud applications, including multifactor authentication
It provides a comprehensive view of security posture across cloud and on-premises resources, combining posture management with workload protection
snapshot.referenceTitle: Microsoft Defender for Cloud Overview — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A software company's monthly Azure bill came in well above forecast. During a cost-review meeting, the team evaluates four candidate actions, and the facts stated in each option have already been confirmed. Which action will NOT reduce the company's Azure bill?
options: Resize several underutilized virtual machines to a smaller size, lowering their hourly rate
Delete managed disks that are no longer attached to any virtual machine
Remove the descriptive tags the team applies to resources for reporting
Move a development workload to a nearby region where the same virtual machine configuration is offered at a lower price
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe factors that can affect costs in Azure — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: An online gift retailer adds extra virtual machines and storage for the December shopping season and removes them in January. December's Azure bill is far higher than February's, although the subscription itself never changed. Which characteristic of Azure pricing explains the difference?
options: Azure follows a consumption-based model: the company pays for the resources used during each billing cycle, so the bill rises and falls with actual usage
Azure recalculates the subscription's tier at the end of each month, and December was billed at a higher tier than February
Azure charges for the peak capacity the subscription could have used during the billing cycle, whether or not that capacity was actually used by any workload
Azure bills a per-deployment fee for each resource created or removed, so the invoice reflects how many deployments were made during the cycle
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe factors that can affect costs in Azure — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A photography platform runs two storage accounts in the same Azure region, each holding a similar volume of photos. One account keeps archives on a cool access tier with limited redundancy; the other serves the galleries from a hot tier with geo-redundant storage. The monthly bills differ noticeably. Which factor explains the difference?
options: The age of each storage account, because Azure applies legacy rates to accounts that were created before the current pricing release came into effect
The settings chosen for each storage account, such as the access tier and how many redundant copies of the data are kept
The subscription that owns each storage account, because every account in a subscription is billed at one shared rate
The tools the teams use to upload photos, because Azure charges storage accounts different rates depending on the upload tool
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe factors that can affect costs in Azure — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A video production company is planning a new rendering service and compares identical virtual machine configurations in two Azure regions using Microsoft's estimation tooling. The estimates show different monthly totals for the same configuration. The company asks what makes the same resource cost different amounts in different regions. Which explanation is correct?
options: The estimate includes a currency conversion fee that Azure adds automatically for regions outside the company's billing country
One region is newer than the other, and Azure temporarily discounts resources provisioned in regions that opened recently
The cost of power, labor, taxes, and fees differs by location, so Azure prices the same resource differently per region
The estimate adds an availability margin that grows with the distance between the chosen region and the location of the company's head office
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe factors that can affect costs in Azure — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: An IT services team decommissioned six virtual machines when a client project ended last quarter, but the following Azure invoices barely decreased. The virtual machines no longer appear anywhere in the subscription. What is the most likely explanation, and what should the team do?
options: Azure keeps billing deleted virtual machines for one full quarter after deletion, and the charges will stop on their own
The subscription still carries a reservation fee for the deleted virtual machines, so the team should open a support request to remove it
Virtual machine charges are invoiced in advance and reconciled later in a separate process, so the team should expect the bill to drop only within a few months
Deleting a virtual machine does not necessarily delete its attached disks and network interfaces, so the team should locate and remove the still-billed leftover resources
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe factors that can affect costs in Azure — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A network engineer at a logistics company is reviewing the data-transfer section of the Azure invoice. Some inbound transfers show no charge, while outbound transfers are grouped by what the invoice calls billing zones. The engineer has worked with availability zones and assumes the two terms refer to the same thing. Which explanation is accurate?
options: Inbound and outbound transfers are both billed at one flat per-gigabyte rate that depends only on the size of the source virtual machine

Some inbound transfers into Azure datacenters are free, while outbound transfers are priced by billing zones — geographic groupings of regions for data-transfer pricing, distinct from availability zones
Transfers are free while they stay inside a single availability zone, and charges apply only when traffic leaves that availability zone
Outbound transfers between Azure regions are free of charge, and data-transfer billing applies only to traffic that leaves Azure entirely to the public internet
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe factors that can affect costs in Azure — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A manufacturer's production database and its reporting virtual machines run continuously, around the clock, with a stable and predictable workload profile. Finance has asked the cloud team to reduce the compute bill without changing the architecture. Which purchasing approach best fits this workload?
options: Buy a Reservation that commits to the specific resource capacity for a one-year or three-year term and applies discounted pricing to matching usage
Use Spot pricing to consume unused Azure capacity at reduced prices, accepting that the workloads can be evicted when Azure needs the capacity back
Commit to an hourly spend amount across eligible compute services with the Azure savings plan for compute, keeping full flexibility over which services consume it
Purchase the database and reporting software through Azure Marketplace, where third-party vendors set the billing and offer reduced rates for continuous use
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe cost optimization options in Azure — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: An event ticketing platform expects a major sales surge. The engineers debate two ways to prepare: scale out by adding identical virtual machine instances, or scale up by moving to larger virtual machines with more cores and memory. The finance lead asks how each strategy would affect the Azure bill. Which explanation is accurate?
options: Both strategies raise only the compute line item of the bill; storage and network charges stay flat no matter how many instances run or how large each one is
Scaling out is billed as one flat platform fee per hour regardless of the instance count, so the total only changes when the fleet scales up to larger virtual machines
Scaling up automatically converts the whole deployment to fixed reservation pricing for the commitment term, while scaling out keeps the standard variable per-usage billing
Scaling out multiplies the number of billed instances — each added virtual machine brings its own compute, storage, and network charges — while scaling up moves each instance to a higher-priced size
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe factors that can affect costs in Azure — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A startup is planning its first Azure solution: a web application with a managed database and object storage. Leadership wants a realistic estimate of the monthly cost before any resources are created. Which tool should the team use?
options: Microsoft Cost Management, after deploying a small pilot of the solution to generate real usage data
Azure Advisor, which forecasts the cost of planned resources before anything is provisioned
The Azure pricing calculator, which estimates the cost of a planned configuration of Azure products
Azure Migrate, which prices new Azure solutions based on an inventory of the company's existing hardware
snapshot.referenceTitle: Explore the pricing calculator — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A junior engineer at a logistics software firm is asked to build an estimate for a planned deployment in the Azure pricing calculator. She hesitates, worried that selecting products for the estimate will create resources on the subscription and start charges. What should her teammates tell her?
options: The pricing calculator is for information purposes only: nothing is provisioned and no services are charged for the items added to an estimate
Products selected in the calculator are provisioned in a stopped state and begin billing only when they are started
Each saved estimate places a one-time estimation fee on the subscription, which is refunded automatically when the estimate is deleted
Estimates act as binding price quotes, so the subscription is charged the estimated amount on the next invoice after the estimate is first saved
snapshot.referenceTitle: Explore the pricing calculator — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A streaming media company is designing a new customer portal. Before deploying anything, the architects want to compare the estimated monthly cost of the planned app service tier, managed database, and storage under two different regions and two redundancy options. Which approach meets this requirement?
options: Deploy a minimal version of the portal in each region and compare the invoices after the first full month
Create a budget for each combination of region and redundancy and compare which budgets raise alerts first during a pilot deployment
Ask Azure Advisor to forecast the cost of each combination of region and redundancy before anything is deployed
Build the planned configuration in the pricing calculator and compare the monthly estimates across the regions and redundancy options
snapshot.referenceTitle: Explore the pricing calculator — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A conglomerate's CFO asks the IT team to use Microsoft's Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) calculator to build the business case for moving workloads to Azure, following a recommendation in an internal document written a few years ago. When the team checks Microsoft's current documentation, what will they find?
options: The TCO calculator is now a built-in view of Microsoft Cost Management that compares on-premises invoices with Azure invoices automatically
The TCO calculator has been retired, and the pricing calculator is the current tool for estimating the cost of Azure resources
The TCO calculator was renamed Azure Migrate, which now produces the official cost estimates for migration projects
The TCO calculator is still available, but access is limited to Enterprise Agreement customers with an active prepayment balance
snapshot.referenceTitle: Explore the pricing calculator — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A healthcare group's Azure spend has grown quickly across several subscriptions. The new finance director wants one place to analyze where the money goes, receive notifications about spending, and set spending limits for the teams. Which capability should the cloud team present first?
options: Microsoft Cost Management, a set of tools to analyze, monitor, and manage Azure costs — including cost reporting, budgets, and alerts
Azure Advisor, which analyzes resources that are already deployed and enforces spending limits on underutilized services
The Azure pricing calculator, which tracks the realized monthly costs of all of the subscriptions in a single consolidated view
Azure Service Health, which sends billing notifications to subscription owners whenever service prices change in their regions
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe the Microsoft Cost Management tool — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A fintech's operations analyst must investigate last month's Azure bill: which services drove the costs, how they accumulated over the month, and whether spending is trending above the team's target. Which Cost Management feature should the analyst open first?
options: Budgets, which visualize historical invoices and automatically forecast the monthly costs of the next billing period for every team in the account
Cost alerts, which display each service's accumulated costs in a daily email digest sent to the subscription owners
Cost analysis, which breaks down costs by subscription, resource group, or service and shows accumulated costs over time against a budget
The pricing calculator, which can reconstruct last month's deployed configuration and calculate the charges it actually incurred
snapshot.referenceTitle: Quickstart: Start using Cost Analysis — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A game studio's nonproduction subscription keeps burning through its monthly allowance without anyone noticing until the invoice arrives. The studio wants spending tracked against a monthly target, and, when the target's threshold is crossed, the affected dev-test resources shut down automatically. Which configuration meets this requirement?
options: A cost analysis view scheduled weekly, which the team reviews to decide manually which resources to stop before the next invoice
A spending cap that Azure Advisor attaches to each individual resource when it detects low utilization, stopping idle resources automatically at the end of each month
A budget on its own, because reaching a budget automatically stops all resource consumption in its scope
A budget with an alert threshold, plus the budget's automation configured to suspend or modify the target resources when the threshold is reached
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe the Microsoft Cost Management tool — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: The research computing lead at a university wants an email sent to the lab's shared mailbox as soon as monthly spending on a production resource group reaches 80% of the agreed amount. Which setup meets this requirement?
options: A budget on the resource group with an alert threshold at 80%, generating a budget alert automatically and emailing the configured recipients when spending reaches it
An Azure Monitor metric alert that watches the resource group's spending and emails the shared mailbox when the metric crosses the 80% mark
A department spending quota alert, which emails the department owners when their spending quota for the period is consumed
A scheduled export of the resource group's cost analysis chart, emailed to the shared mailbox on the first day of every month
snapshot.referenceTitle: Tutorial: Create and manage budgets — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: An automotive supplier with an Enterprise Agreement funds its Azure usage with Azure Prepayment, previously called monetary commitment. The billing administrator wants alerts that fire as the prepayment balance is drawn down. Which Cost Management alert type serves this purpose, and how does it behave?
options: Budget alerts, which the billing team must generate manually from the cost alerts page on a weekly schedule
Credit alerts, which are generated automatically at 90% and 100% of the Azure credit balance
Department spending quota alerts, which fire automatically when any subscription in the enrollment exceeds its assigned spending quota
Invoice alerts, which are raised when the monthly invoice consumes the remaining prepayment balance on the account
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe the Microsoft Cost Management tool — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: After a busy quarter, a marketing agency's Azure bill is far above expectations. The environment includes many development and test virtual machines that are suspected to sit idle most of the time. The team wants personalized recommendations that identify underutilized resources and suggest concrete ways to reduce spend. Which capability should they use?
options: The pricing calculator, which flags resources in the current configuration whose estimated cost is above the account average
Budgets, which recommend which virtual machines should be shut down once the monthly spending threshold is crossed
Azure Advisor cost recommendations, which analyze resource utilization and recommend, for example, shutting down or resizing low-utilization virtual machines
Cost analysis, which automatically proposes configuration changes whenever the costs inside a resource group rise above their recent trend
snapshot.referenceTitle: Optimize virtual machine (VM) or virtual machine scale set (VMSS) spend by resizing or shutting down underutilized instances — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A holding company runs workloads for two independent business units in a single Azure subscription. Each unit must now receive its own Azure invoice, and each unit's costs must be reported separately. What should the company do?
options: Keep the single subscription and attach a business-unit tag to every resource, so the invoices are split by tag at the end of each month
Create a separate resource group for each business unit, because Azure issues one invoice per resource group in a subscription
Create a management group for each business unit, because Azure issues one invoice per management group in the organization
Create a separate subscription for each business unit, so each unit's usage is billed and reported at its own subscription scope
snapshot.referenceTitle: Overview of Billing — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A fast-growing SaaS provider wants a lightweight way to attach structured information — such as environment, owner, and cost center — to its Azure resources so they can be organized, searched, and reported on. Which statement describes the construct the team should use?
options: Resource locks, which label resources with metadata and prevent the labels from being changed by other administrators
Resource tags, which are name-value pairs that add metadata to resources for organization and reporting
Management groups, which attach key-value metadata to every subscription that sits beneath them in the hierarchy
Resource groups, which store a fixed set of metadata fields for each resource they contain when it is created
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe the purpose of tags — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: An engineering consultancy keeps all of its Azure resources in one subscription, with resource groups organized by application. Finance now needs monthly cost reports by internal cost center, a categorization that cuts across applications, without reorganizing how the applications are grouped. How should the consultancy meet this requirement?
options: Apply a cost center tag to each resource and group costs by that tag in cost reporting
Move the resources into new resource groups so that each resource group maps to a single cost center
Create a new subscription for each cost center and migrate the resources accordingly
Use Azure Policy to assign each resource to a cost center at the subscription level
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe the purpose of tags — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A streaming provider's platform team runs a maintenance pipeline that must execute a task against every resource belonging to one specific workload. The resources of that workload are spread across multiple resource groups and subscriptions. Which approach lets the pipeline select exactly those resources reliably?
options: Match resources by name prefix, because every resource of the workload is expected to follow the team's naming convention
Keep a list of the resource groups that contain workload resources and treat group membership as the selector
Apply resource locks to the workload's resources so the pipeline can find them by their lock status
Apply a workload tag to the resources and have the pipeline query for, and act on, the resources carrying that tag
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe the purpose of tags — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: An insurer's cloud governance team publishes a tagging standard: every new resource must carry an owner tag, and tags that are accidentally removed should be restored. Manual reviews keep missing violations. Which mechanism should the team use to enforce the standard?
options: Apply the owner tag to each resource group and rely on the resources inheriting it automatically
Put a resource lock on every resource so that its tags can no longer be removed
Use Azure Policy to require the owner tag on provisioned resources and to reapply tags that have been removed
Export the full resource inventory every week and have a script email the owners of resources that are missing the tag
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe the purpose of tags — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A retail chain's architect applies the tag CostCenter=100 to a resource group that contains several virtual machines. A later inventory report that lists each virtual machine's own tags shows none of them carrying the cost center. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The tag will appear on the virtual machines within 24 hours, once Azure's tag synchronization job completes its daily run
Tags applied to a resource group are not automatically applied to the resources inside it — each level carries its own tags
The virtual machines reject the tag because their current SKU does not support cost center metadata on this resource type
The tag was applied in a different region from the virtual machines, so it cannot reach any of the resources outside of its own region
snapshot.referenceTitle: Use tags to organize your Azure resources and management hierarchy — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A pharmaceutical company on an Enterprise Agreement enables the tag inheritance setting in Microsoft Cost Management. Its resource groups carry cost center tags, but most child resources have no tags of their own. Which statement describes what changes once the setting takes effect?
options: Subscription and resource group tags are applied to child resources' usage records in cost data, enabling grouping by tag while resources stay untagged
Every child resource immediately receives the inherited tags on its own properties, including resources that were created years before the setting was enabled
Only resources created after the setting is enabled inherit the resource group tags, while existing resources stay excluded from any grouping
Inherited tags override any tags already applied directly to a resource in every case where the two values differ from each other
snapshot.referenceTitle: Group and allocate costs using tag inheritance — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A national hospital network keeps clinical and operational data in several places: an on-premises SQL Server instance, Azure data services, and a third-party software-as-a-service analytics platform. The newly hired chief data officer wants a single solution that provides one unified view of all this data and helps govern it. Which service should the chief data officer choose?
options: Microsoft Purview, which provides a single, unified view into data across on-premises, multicloud, and software-as-a-service environments
Azure Arc, which extends Azure resource management to servers and clusters that run outside of Azure
Azure Monitor, which collects and analyzes telemetry such as metrics and logs from applications and infrastructure
Azure Policy, which enforces organizational standards and evaluates the compliance of Azure resources
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe the purpose of Microsoft Purview — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: Analysts at an online retailer waste hours every week asking engineers where datasets live and what each column means. The data team wants a governed, searchable experience where business users can discover available data assets, understand what they need to know about them, and get secure access. Which solution should the team choose?
options: The catalog experience in Microsoft Purview, which helps data consumers find, understand, and access data securely
Azure Data Factory, which builds pipelines that copy and transform data between sources and destinations
Azure Data Share, which distributes data assets to external partners and other outside organizations
Azure Synapse Analytics, which consolidates data from across the company into a single warehouse for large-scale reporting
snapshot.referenceTitle: Learn about Microsoft Purview Unified Catalog — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: An external auditor is questioning the figures in a logistics company's quarterly fuel-cost report and asks exactly how each number was derived. The data platform team must show the data's full journey — from the source systems through every transformation to the final report. Which Microsoft Purview capability should the team use?
options: Data Lifecycle Management, which retains and deletes records according to a defined retention schedule
Data Loss Prevention, which blocks sensitive data from leaving the organization through sharing
End-to-end data lineage, which traces how data flows from sources through every transformation to consumers
Sensitive data classification, which labels data assets that contain regulated information
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe the purpose of Microsoft Purview — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A compliance officer at an insurance group must build an inventory of where sensitive information — such as policyholders' identification numbers and health details — is stored across databases, file shares, and on-premises systems. She wants automated scanning that discovers this data and applies classification across the whole estate. Which service meets this requirement?
options: Microsoft Defender for Cloud, which assesses the security posture of cloud workloads and issues recommendations
Azure Migrate, which discovers on-premises servers and assesses their readiness for migration
Azure Policy, which audits resource configurations against organizational standards
Microsoft Purview, which scans data sources across the estate and applies sensitive data classification
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe the purpose of Microsoft Purview — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A streaming media company is defining its governance program. The platform team must enforce rules on Azure resources, such as deploying only to approved regions. Separately, the data office must discover, catalog, and classify company data wherever it lives — in Azure, in other clouds, and on-premises. Which pairing of services meets both requirements?
options: Microsoft Purview to enforce the resource rules, and Azure Policy to discover, catalog, and classify the data
Azure Policy to enforce the resource rules, and Microsoft Purview to discover, catalog, and classify the data
Azure Policy for both requirements, because policy definitions can evaluate the data stored inside resources
Microsoft Purview for both requirements, because its data map can deny the creation of noncompliant resources
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe the purpose of Microsoft Purview — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: During onboarding week at an energy utility, a newly hired cloud engineer is asked to summarize Microsoft Purview for the rest of the team. Several teammates currently confuse it with other governance services in Azure. Which statement about Microsoft Purview is accurate?
options: Microsoft Purview enforces organizational standards on Azure resources and can prevent noncompliant resources from being created
Microsoft Purview locks critical resources so that not even administrators can update or delete them
Microsoft Purview builds a unified data map of the organization's entire data estate, spanning on-premises, multicloud, and software-as-a-service sources
Microsoft Purview forecasts cloud spending by subscription and raises alerts when budgets are exceeded
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe the purpose of Microsoft Purview — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: The IT operations lead at a university must ensure that resources across several Azure subscriptions follow institutional standards — for example, only approved virtual machine sizes and required tags — and must be able to show auditors which resources comply. Which service is designed for this need?
options: Azure Policy, which evaluates resources against your rules and reports each resource's compliance state
Azure role-based access control (RBAC), which controls which users can perform actions on each resource
Resource locks, which prevent resources from being deleted or changed
Azure Monitor, which collects metrics and activity logs for operational insight
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe the purpose of Azure Policy — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A fintech's platform team has drafted a policy that requires every storage account to carry an Owner tag. Before enforcing the rule, they want to track how it would affect existing and new resources without blocking anyone's deployments. Which policy effect should they start with?
options: Deny, so that any request missing the tag is rejected
Modify, so that the missing tag is added to every request automatically
Audit, so that noncompliant resources are recorded in the compliance results without being blocked
Disabled, so that the definition exists in the environment but is never evaluated
snapshot.referenceTitle: Overview of Azure Policy — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: The security team at a manufacturing company must guarantee that no new virtual machine can be created outside the company's approved Azure regions — an attempt to create a VM in another region has to fail. Which effect should the team's policy assignment use?
options: Audit, which lets the VM be created and then flags it as noncompliant
Deny, which blocks the creation request so the noncompliant VM is never created
Modify, which changes the requested region to an approved location before the VM is created
AuditIfNotExists, which checks the VM after deployment and logs a noncompliance record
snapshot.referenceTitle: Overview of Azure Policy — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A cloud architect at a public-sector agency needs to roll out a security baseline made of many related policy definitions — allowed locations, required tags, and allowed virtual machine SKUs. The definitions must be assigned and tracked together as a single item, and more definitions may be added later without creating extra assignments. What should the architect create?
options: A management group, which bundles the policies for all subscriptions beneath it
One large custom policy definition that contains all of the individual rules
A separate assignment for each policy definition, so each can be tracked on its own
An initiative definition, which groups the policy definitions for assignment and tracking as a set
snapshot.referenceTitle: Overview of Azure Policy — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A holding company organizes its Azure environment under a management group that contains multiple subscriptions. Governance staff want a single policy assignment that covers every subscription and all resources inside them — including resources created in the future. Where should the assignment be created?
options: At the management group scope, because all child subscriptions and their resources inherit the assignment
At each subscription separately, because policy assignments are never inherited across scopes
At each resource group, because policies apply only within the resource group where they're assigned
At the individual resource scope, because Azure Policy evaluates resources one by one
snapshot.referenceTitle: Overview of Azure Policy — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: An administrator at a food delivery company has assigned a policy that requires an Environment tag on resources. The director now asks for a list of the resources that are missing the tag. Where should the administrator look for this information?
options: Azure Advisor, which recommends best practices for cost, performance, reliability, and security
Azure Service Health, which lists Azure service incidents and planned maintenance
Azure Monitor activity logs, which record the operations performed on each resource over time
The compliance results in Azure Policy, which show each resource as compliant or noncompliant
snapshot.referenceTitle: Overview of Azure Policy — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A software company requires every new Azure resource to carry a CostCenter tag. Deployments that omit the tag must not be rejected — instead, Azure should add the tag with a default value during the create or update request. Which effect should the policy definition use?
options: Audit, which records the resource as noncompliant in the results and leaves the tag missing
Modify, which adds the required tag with its default value when the request omits it
Deny, which rejects any request that doesn't already include the tag
DeployIfNotExists, which deploys a related resource when the tag is absent
snapshot.referenceTitle: Overview of Azure Policy — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A junior cloud administrator at a startup asks a senior engineer to clarify the difference between Azure RBAC and Azure Policy. The senior engineer explains that Azure RBAC controls which actions each user can perform. According to that explanation, what does Azure Policy control?
options: Which users are allowed to read the data that is stored inside each Azure resource
The properties resources can have, such as locations, SKUs, and tags, regardless of who creates them
Which users are allowed to delete each resource in the subscription
The prices and budget limits that apply to each resource
snapshot.referenceTitle: Overview of Azure Policy — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A subscription-level policy assignment blocks the creation of networking resources everywhere in a research organization's subscription. A new dedicated resource group must be exempt from this rule so the networking team can create resources there, while the policy continues to apply everywhere else. What should the administrator do?
options: Delete the assignment and recreate it on every other resource group individually
Grant the networking team Owner permissions on the new resource group, which bypasses the policy for them
Update the assignment so the new resource group is excluded from the policy's scope
Apply a CanNotDelete lock to the new resource group, which stops policy evaluation inside it
snapshot.referenceTitle: Overview of Azure Policy — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: An airline's subscription contains hundreds of virtual machines, several of which use unapproved VM sizes. An administrator assigns a new Audit-effect policy that permits only approved sizes, and assumes it will affect only virtual machines created from now on. What actually happens to the existing noncompliant VMs?
options: They're never evaluated, because Azure Policy applies only to resources created after the assignment exists
They're automatically resized to an approved SKU, because Audit remediates noncompliant resources
The assignment fails, because the subscription already contains noncompliant resources
They're evaluated and flagged as noncompliant in the policy's compliance results
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe the purpose of Azure Policy — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: During a cleanup sprint at a utilities company, an operator deleted the wrong resource group and caused a production outage. Management asks for the simplest built-in guardrail that prevents anyone from accidentally deleting the critical production database, while normal configuration changes must continue. What should the team apply?
options: A ReadOnly lock, which blocks both updates and deletions of the database
A Delete (CanNotDelete) lock, which lets authorized users modify the database but blocks its deletion
A tag named Protection with the value DoNotDelete, which marks the database as critical
An Azure Policy assignment with the Audit effect, which reports any attempt to delete the database
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe the purpose of resource locks — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A pharmacy chain's production database server has a Delete (CanNotDelete) lock applied. An authorized database engineer needs to apply a routine configuration update to the server. What happens when the engineer submits the change?
options: The update succeeds, because a Delete lock still allows authorized users to modify the resource
The update fails, because every resource lock blocks all write operations on the resource
The update succeeds only after the engineer asks the subscription Owner to remove the lock
The update fails, because a Delete lock freezes the resource configuration until the lock expires
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe the purpose of resource locks — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: An external audit at a pension fund requires that, for the next 60 days, nobody may change or delete the resources used by the claims system in any way, though auditors must still be able to view them. Which lock level meets this requirement?
options: CanNotDelete, because it blocks changes and deletions while still allowing reads
CanNotDelete, because it blocks deletions while still allowing configuration changes
ReadOnly, because it allows reads but blocks both updates and deletions
ReadOnly, because it allows authorized administrators to keep updating the resources
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe the purpose of resource locks — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A media company wants to protect all resources in its production subscription from accidental deletion with a single lock, while day-to-day configuration changes must keep working. New resources are added to the subscription constantly. What should the company do?
options: Apply a Delete (CanNotDelete) lock at the subscription scope, so all existing and future resources inherit it
Apply a Delete lock to each resource individually, because locks affect only the resource they're created on
Apply a Delete lock at the management group above the subscription, because management groups are the highest lockable scope
Apply a ReadOnly lock at the subscription scope, so the resources stay protected while updates continue
snapshot.referenceTitle: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: At a mining company, a subscription Owner with full Azure RBAC permissions tries to delete a storage account that has a CanNotDelete lock, and the operation fails. A colleague insists the lock must be misconfigured, because Owner permissions should override it. Which explanation is correct?
options: The lock is misconfigured, because Owner permissions always take precedence over resource locks
The storage account is being blocked by Azure Policy, so the Owner needs a policy exemption
Owners can delete locked resources from PowerShell or the Azure CLI, just not from the portal
Resource locks apply regardless of RBAC permissions — even an Owner must remove the lock before deleting
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe the purpose of resource locks — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: To reduce accidental deletions, a team lead at an e-commerce company proposes applying a tag named Lock with the value DoNotDelete to every production resource, expecting Azure to block deletions automatically. What is the best response to this proposal?
options: The tag will work, provided it's applied by a user with Owner permissions
The tag won't block anything — tags are metadata for organizing and reporting, so a Delete lock should be applied instead
The tag will work as long as child resources inherit it from the resource group
The tag won't block anything, but a policy with the Modify effect could enforce it as a deletion guard
snapshot.referenceTitle: Use tags to organize your Azure resources and management hierarchy — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: An administrator at a bank applies a ReadOnly lock to a production storage account. An automation tool that previously listed the account's access keys to connect now fails on that step, even though listing keys looks like a read-only action. Why did the lock block this operation?
options: ReadOnly locks on storage accounts also block all data operations on blobs and queues
The tool's service principal no longer has the Reader role on the storage account
The List Keys operation is a POST request, and a ReadOnly lock blocks requests that aren't read-type
The lock disabled the account keys, so only Microsoft Entra credentials work from now on
snapshot.referenceTitle: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A database administrator applies a ReadOnly lock to the logical server that hosts a critical Azure SQL database and tells management the data is now protected against loss. Management asks whether the lock also prevents data inside the database from being modified or deleted. What is the correct answer?
options: No — locks apply to control-plane operations, so creating, updating, and deleting data inside the database is still possible
Yes — a ReadOnly lock blocks every operation on the server, including data changes
Yes — locks protect both the resource and the data it contains, so no backup is needed
No — but applying a CanNotDelete lock instead would protect the data while allowing configuration changes
snapshot.referenceTitle: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement: A payment-processing company defines two requirements: (1) the production payments database must be protected against accidental deletion by anyone — including administrators — while administrators keep their current permissions and routine configuration changes continue; and (2) any new storage account must be created only in approved regions. Which combination meets both requirements?
options: A ReadOnly lock on the database, and an Azure Policy assignment with the Deny effect for allowed locations
A Delete (CanNotDelete) lock on the database, and an Azure Policy assignment with the Audit effect for allowed locations
A DoNotDelete tag on the database, and an Azure RBAC role that removes delete permissions from administrators
A Delete (CanNotDelete) lock on the database, and an Azure Policy assignment with the Deny effect for allowed locations
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe the purpose of resource locks — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
A regional bank has opened its first Azure subscription. The IT operations team includes administrators with no scripting background who prefer working visually. During onboarding, they ask what the Azure portal offers them.

Which statement describes the Azure portal?
options: A desktop application that administrators must install on their workstations before they can manage Azure resources
A browser-based shell where administrators run Bash or PowerShell commands to manage Azure resources
A web-based, unified console that provides a graphical interface for building, managing, and monitoring Azure resources
A command-line executable that automates deployments by processing JSON definition files
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is the Azure portal? — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
A data analyst at an online education company starts every workday in the Azure portal by opening the same handful of resources: a web app, its database, and two virtual machines. She wants all of them to appear together as soon as she signs in.

What should she do in the Azure portal?
options: Customize a dashboard with the resources she monitors and set that dashboard as her startup page
Place the resources in a management group and open that group's page each morning
Bookmark each resource's page in her web browser and open the bookmarks one by one
Export the resources into an Azure PowerShell script that lists them at the start of each day

snapshot.statement:
A small design agency is deciding which Azure management tool fits each kind of task. The agency owner is comfortable with visual tools and wants to understand where the Azure portal is the right choice.

Which task is the best fit for the Azure portal?
options: Running an unattended nightly job that creates and then deletes dozens of temporary test resources
Exploring a new Azure service and creating a single storage account with the help of guided wizards
Deploying identical environments across many different subscriptions from one repeatable definition file
Governing on-premises servers in the agency's own datacenter as if they were Azure resources
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is the Azure portal? — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
During onboarding at a logistics company, a new operations engineer asks how the team runs Azure commands without installing anything on their laptops.

Which statement describes Azure Cloud Shell?
options: A desktop application that gives each administrator a graphical copy of the Azure console on their workstation
A command-line tool that can only be installed on computers that run a Linux distribution
A JSON file format used to declare the resources that a deployment will create in Azure
An interactive, authenticated, browser-accessible terminal for managing Azure resources, offering a choice of Bash or PowerShell
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Azure Cloud Shell? — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
The platform engineers at a video streaming startup are fluent in Bash scripting on Linux but have never used PowerShell. They want a command-line tool they can run from their own terminals to manage Azure resources.

Which tool is the best fit for the team?
options: Azure PowerShell, because it can automate management tasks that the Azure CLI cannot
Azure CLI, because its Bash-based command syntax matches the team's existing scripting experience
Azure Cloud Shell, because it is the only environment where the Azure CLI can run
Azure PowerShell, because the Azure CLI cannot be installed on Linux workstations
snapshot.referenceTitle: Describe tools for interacting with Azure — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
An insurance company is writing an internal quick-reference guide about its Azure management tools. The documentation owner asks for one accurate sentence about Azure PowerShell.

Which statement should the guide include?
options: A product consisting of official PowerShell modules whose cmdlets manage Azure resources by calling the Azure REST APIs
A Bash-based command-line tool that can only be installed on computers running a Linux distribution
A graphical console in the Azure portal that records the manual steps of each configuration change
A browser-accessible terminal that runs cmdlets but cannot be installed on local machines
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Azure PowerShell — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
An auditor at a public-sector agency occasionally runs a few Azure PowerShell cmdlets from different shared workstations. She wants a shell that is already signed in with her Azure account and permissions, requires no installation, and asks for no separate login step.

Which tool meets these requirements?
options: Install the Az PowerShell module on each workstation and run a sign-in command before every session
Use the Azure portal's guided wizards to perform equivalent changes without running cmdlets
Use Azure Cloud Shell, which authenticates automatically with the Azure credentials of the signed-in user
Use Azure Arc to project her workstations into Azure and run cmdlets on them from there
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is Azure Cloud Shell? — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
An energy company is preparing an internal comparison of Azure command-line tools, and the author needs an accurate definition of the Azure CLI.

Which statement accurately describes the Azure CLI?
options: A Windows-only executable that reproduces the Azure portal's guided wizards in a console window
A PowerShell module whose cmdlets can only run inside Windows PowerShell on Windows machines
An interactive terminal that requires an Azure Files share before any command can run
A cross-platform command-line tool for connecting to Azure and executing administrative commands, interactively or in scripts
snapshot.referenceTitle: What is the Azure CLI? — Microsoft Learn

snapshot.statement:
Two engineers at a manufacturing firm are comparing Azure command-line tools before the team standardizes on one. One argues that the tools serve different workload sizes; the other disagrees and wants a definitive statement for the team's standards document.

Which statement accurately compares Azure PowerShell and the Azure CLI?
options: They are functionally equivalent for managing Azure resources, and teams generally choose based on the shell they already know
The Azure CLI is built for large automated deployments, while Azure PowerShell is limited to small interactive tasks
Azure PowerShell can be used only inside Azure Cloud Shell, while the Azure CLI can be installed locally
The two tools send requests through different management APIs, so their capabilities differ from tool to tool
